docs.title: tsfm-trl
docs.text:
Time-series foundation models behind one API — and an honest map of what each architecture can actually do in a given environment.

tsfm-trl is first a benchmark and compatibility harness: 46 open TSFM checkpoints (Chronos family, TimesFM 2.x/2.5/3.0, Moirai 1.1/2.0/MoE, MOMENT, TTM, Toto, Time-MoE, Sundial, Kronos, TiRex, Kairos, Timestral, Hirondel, t0, FlowState, VisionTS, Aurora, Yug, plus statistical baselines) loaded through one adapter contract, then driven through the same set of tasks. Post-training (fine-tune, probing, reward/RL) sits on top of that contract — it is a capability gate, not a claim that any model got better.

docs.title: The two claims this library keeps apart
docs.text:
question produced by can be quoted as compatibility does this architecture load, forecast, emit quantiles, embed, classify, detect anomalies, take post-training — in this environment? tsfm-trl doctor → measured matrix yes, with the machine and env in the row effectiveness how accurate is it? tsfm-trl evaluate → RMSE/MASE/CRPS/WQL/coverage yes, per the protocol capability smoke does a training step run at all? doctor's fine-tune/reward columns only as "it runs", never as "it helps"

Mixing the third into the first is the most common way a TSFM table becomes misleading, so the matrix labels it separately and the fine-tune cell says what its numbers mean.

docs.title: Quick tour
docs.text:
pip install -e .                       # core only; per-family venvs: scripts/make_envs.sh

tsfm-trl list --tier A                 # what the registry knows about
tsfm-trl forecast --model chronos-t5-small --horizon 21 --md
tsfm-trl evaluate --model toto-2-22m --horizons 21,63,126 --max-windows 32

tsfm-trl classify --model moirai-2.0-R-small --label dir5 --routes probe,head,native
tsfm-trl reward  --model chronos-t5-small --steps 48 --peft lora --mode auto

tsfm-trl doctor --all-envs --json reports/matrix.json      # the compatibility matrix
tsfm-trl doctor --merge reports/*.json --md COMPATIBILITY.md

docs.title: Measured compatibility (2026-11-21, 46 models, two machines)
docs.text:
task ok declined by the model failed not checked load 45 0 1 0 forecast / predict 44 0 1 1 quantiles 35 9 0 2 embed 44 0 1 1 classify 44 0 1 1 anomaly 44 1 0 1 reward / RL 30 15 0 1 fine-tune (capability) 29 9 0 8

The two red cells are named, not averaged away: VisionTS++ (the Hub repo ships .ckpt weights only, the upstream package is not installable as a package) and TiRex-2 (the vendor's Triton mLSTM scan kernel compiles at import and then fails at runtime on CUDA 13 / sm100, and the native fallback's JIT-built extension does not import — see known issues).

declined means the model or its public package has no path for that task here (TimesFM's build is inference-only, Moirai 1.1's forward samples instead of returning differentiable quantiles). failed means something was attempted and broke, with the reason captured in the row. History says to doubt failed before believing declined: three "the model cannot be fine-tuned" verdicts in this project turned out to be our bugs.

docs.title: Which post-training path each architecture exposes
docs.text:
path models requirement grpo 2 (Chronos-T5 small/base) token log-probabilities over its own sampled paths rft 18 can sample candidate paths; no log-prob needed descent 5 differentiable quantile head descent·pt 5 differentiable point head only — 15 no trainable path in the public build

GRPO here is hand-written (~435 lines in tsfm_trl/training/reward.py), with no RL library dependency; only two architectures expose the token log-probs that true GRPO needs, which is a property of the vendor builds and not something the harness papers over. Details in RL / reward API and Reward & RL paths.

docs.title: Two installs, not one
docs.text:
# the library (any python 3.10–3.12)
uv venv envs/core && uv pip install --python envs/core/bin/python -e .

# the families that cannot share that interpreter
./scripts/make_envs.sh                       # every env declared in envs/envs.toml
./scripts/make_envs.sh core moirai moment    # or a subset

The library's own dependency floor is small:

numpy>=1.24 pandas>=2.0 scikit-learn>=1.3 scipy statsmodels>=0.14
pyyaml pyarrow huggingface_hub safetensors tqdm

Everything that models need lives in the per-family environments (described in envs/README.md, machine-readable in envs/envs.toml). doctor --all-envs runs each registry row in its declared env, so a resolver fight between uni2ts, momentfm, betatool and neuralforecast never happens.

docs.title: torch is platform-specific, so it is pinned separately
docs.text:
make_envs.sh installs torch from TORCH_SPEC / TORCH_INDEX instead of the lock:

# x86 + CUDA 12.x
./scripts/make_envs.sh core
# DGX Spark (aarch64, GB10, CUDA 13) — plain PyPI aarch64 wheels are already cu13
TORCH_SPEC=torch ./scripts/make_envs.sh core moirai moment timemoe tirex tirex2 kronos sundial

The locks (envs/*.lock.txt) are frozen from venvs where the matrix actually passed, and are installed with --no-deps: their metadata is mutually contradictory (gluonts asks for pandas<2.2; the working venv carries 2.3.3), and re-resolving would refuse a configuration that is known to run.

docs.title: Weights
docs.text:
export TSFM_WEIGHTS_ROOT=$HOME/models
./scripts/prefetch_weights.py --tier A         # 20 rows; 5 rows have no public weights

ModelHub resolves a registry id in this order: $TSFM_WEIGHTS_ROOT/<org>/<name>, then the matching directory anywhere under $TSFM_WEIGHTS_ROOT, then the Hugging Face cache, then the Hub. Downloading during a measurement is why prefetching is a separate step: a row that pulls 5 GB mid-run skews its timing and hides an offline failure as a "model bug".

docs.title: Third-party checkouts (no wheel, code only in git)
docs.text:
Kronos, Sundial and VisionTS++ publish weights on the Hub but their code lives only in a repository. Clone them anywhere and point the library at them:

git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/shiyu-coder/Kronos        $HOME/third_party/Kronos
git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/thuml/Sundial            $HOME/third_party/Sundial
git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/InfiniteZZZ/VisionTS     $HOME/third_party/VisionTS
export TSFMTRL_THIRD_PARTY=$HOME/third_party

tsfm_trl/thirdparty.py puts those directories (and their subdirectories, plus ./third_party/* and ./envs/*) on sys.path. Note the orgs differ per family: the Kronos code is shiyu-coder/Kronos, while its weights live under the NeoQuasar/ HF org. When an import fails, the error names the missing checkout and prints the git clone line — a missing repo is reported as an environment gap, never as a model failure.

docs.text: machine what it proved laptop, RTX Ada 6 GB, CUDA 12.x development, core/moirai/moment/toto/tirex/timemoe/kronos/ttm envs DGX Spark (GB10, aarch64, 119 GB unified) the aarch64 matrix; TiRex-2's Triton path (sm ≥ 10.0, Triton ≥ 3.4) 3× A6000 (escalation) not needed so far: every Tier-A row fit on 6–48 GB at smoke size

docs.title: The parquet engine is an environment dependency, not a model one
docs.text:
The canonical benchmark series are train/validation/test parquet directories, so every family env that should be able to read a dataset needs a parquet engine. Two pins collide: envs frozen on numpy 1.26 cannot import pyarrow ≥ 18 (pyarrow requires NumPy 2.0 or newer), and pandas' fallback names fastparquet, which is not what you should install into a frozen env. Use the version the numpy pin allows —

uv pip install --python envs/sundial/bin/python --no-deps pyarrow==16.1.0   # numpy 1.26 envs
uv pip install --python envs/core/bin/python     --no-deps pyarrow==26.0.1  # numpy 2 envs

SeriesDataset._from_dir now raises a DataError that says exactly this instead of letting pandas' optional-dependency message read like a model failure.

docs.title: One call, one contract
docs.text:
from tsfm_trl import ModelHub
m = ModelHub.load("chronos-2", device="cuda", ctx_cap=2048, batch=16)
pred = m.predict([ctx_a, ctx_b], horizon=63)

Pred is the same object for every family:

field shape point (B, H) median/mean forecast, always quantiles (B, H, len(LEVELS)) or None resampled onto the canonical grid LEVELS samples (B, K, H) or None sample paths when the model exposes them meta dict how the interval was produced, normalisation, backend/kernel choice 
from tsfm_trl.model.base import LEVELS     # (0.1 … 0.9) canonical grid
pred.quantile(0.9)                          # (B, H) column of the canonical grid

Adapters call to_levels(q, their_levels) on the way out, so TiRex's 100-quantile grid, TimesFM's 9-quantile grid and Moirai's 0.1-0.9 head all become comparable. A model that emits no distribution sets quantiles = None (MOMENT's mean head, small TTM releases, the statistical baselines) rather than inventing one.

Contexts are trimmed by trim() to max_context, aligned to the model's patch step, and pandas objects are coerced with data.series.as_1d (a DataFrame under np.asarray iterates column names, which is where "could not convert string to float: 'close'" comes from).

docs.title: Evaluation
docs.text:
from tsfm_trl.eval.evaluate import forecast_eval
from tsfm_trl.eval.metrics import forecast_report

rows = forecast_eval(m, ds, horizons=(21, 63), spans=("test",), max_windows=64)
print(forecast_report(rows))

Point metrics: mae, rmse, mape, smape, mase, nd, directional_accuracy, rank_corr. Distribution metrics: pinball, wql, crps_from_quantiles, quantile_coverage, and relative_skill to compare against a baseline row.

Two honesty rules:

  • quantile_coverage counts only the bands the model emits. A model whose grid stops at 0.9 must not be credited with 95 % coverage.
  • Anchor-relative error (nd, mase) is the default comparison, because on price panels absolute MAE is dominated by the series' own scale. See 07_finance_tasks.md.

docs.title: Multi-step longer than one patch
docs.text:
Patch-output models (TiRex/TiRex-2) produce a fixed patch per forward. The adapters do a median-rollback rollout — forecast, append the median, forecast again — and record it:

pred.meta["rollout_steps"]   # e.g. 3 for horizon 96 with a 32-step patch

so a table reader knows a 96-step TiRex row is a rollout, not a single decode.

docs.title: Baselines are part of the matrix
docs.text: naive, seasonal_naive, theta, arima, moving_average are registered models in the same registry. They exist so a "✅ fine-tune" on a 300 M TSFM can be compared with something that costs nothing, and so a metric bug shows up immediately (a TSFM that loses to seasonal naive on a synthetic fixture is a measurement bug). theta is implemented in-house because statsmodels never shipped ThetaModel despite promising it since 0.12.

docs.title: Anomaly
docs.text: m.anomaly_scores(contexts) is model-native when the family has a reconstruction or residual path (MOMENT, Moirai, Toto), and otherwise a documented fallback: the forecast residual under the model's own interval (or a context-scaled z-score when the model has no interval), with supports["anomaly"] stating which one produced it.

docs.title: 3 · Fine-tuning
docs.text:
Why this exists in a benchmark harness. Fine-tuning is not the deliverable and the matrix's fine-tune column is not a result. It is a capability gate: for each architecture we prove there is a differentiable objective — the vendor's own where one exists — that gradients flow through, that a trainable subset can be selected, and that the run is checkpointable with provenance. That gate is what makes adapted rows in a benchmark table auditable (which base, which PEFT level, which parameters, which split boundary). Accuracy comparisons live in docs/09_benchmark.md; nothing in this file or in the matrix claims fine-tuning improves out-of-sample skill.

from tsfm_trl import ForecastTrainer, ModelHub, TrainingConfig
from tsfm_trl.data.fixtures import tiny_finance

m   = ModelHub.load("moirai-2.0-R-small", device="cuda")
cfg = TrainingConfig(budget="fs16", peft="lora", ctx=256, horizon=16, seed=0)
res = ForecastTrainer(m, cfg).fit(tiny_finance())

res.status, res.steps, res.loss_first, res.loss_last   # 'smoke', 8, 3.027, 3.111
res.checkpoint                                          # written path

CLI equivalent:

tsfm-trl fit --model moirai-2.0-R-small --series px.csv --peft lora --budget fs16 \
             --ctx 256 --horizon 16 --ckpt reports/ft/px

docs.title: Data
docs.text:
fit accepts any of:

  • a SeriesDataset (or a CSV/Parquet path, or a DataFrame) — windows are built for you with a train/val/test split,
  • {"windows": [(ctx, y), ...], "info": {...}} — pre-cut windows, what the matrix uses,
  • {"dataset": ds} — explicit.

Windows come from data.series.windows(values, horizon, ctx, stride=…); the split index is stored in the checkpoint so an evaluation can never accidentally train on the test span.

docs.title: How much to train: budgets, not step counts
docs.text:
TrainingConfig(budget=...) picks a size, and the trainer keeps the shape of the run stable across families:

budget windows steps lr fs16 (default for the matrix) 16 40 (≤ that) 1e-5 fs64 64 120 1e-5 full all 3 epochs 5e-6

smoke=True caps steps to 3 — that is what doctor uses, because the matrix checks that a fine-tune runs, not that it converges. Losses are still reported (✅ (0.587→0.612)), so a diverging run is visible rather than hidden.

docs.title: Three levels of invasiveness
docs.text:
TrainingConfig(peft="heads_only")   # only the forecast head(s) train
TrainingConfig(peft="lora", lora_r=8, lora_targets=["q", "v"])
TrainingConfig(peft="full")         # everything (fine on ≤300 M at smoke size)
  • heads_only uses the adapter's head_prefixes (e.g. ("decoder", "projection", "head", "p21") for Kairos) — the names come from the vendor modules, and the list that actually became trainable is stored in the checkpoint.
  • lora goes through training.peft.apply_lora, and it freezes the trunk first. It did not always: _inject froze only the nn.Linears it wrapped, while every HF checkpoint loads with requires_grad=True, so peft="lora" had been "full fine-tune plus a few adapters" for most families — t0-gamma reported 156 M trainable parameters, which is its trunk, not an adapter budget. A frozen trunk plus adapters is what a LoRA budget means; the current counts are 1.08 M for chronos-t5-small, 2.57 M for MOMENT-1-large, 59.6 k for TTM-r2. merge_lora folds adapters into the base weights for export.
  • full is refused for families where the backbone cannot take a gradient (see below).

Loss follows the model: loss_kind = "quantile" families are trained with pinball on their own head, "token" families (Chronos-T5, Time-MoE, Kronos) with cross-entropy on their discrete tokens, and vendor-loop families (Kronos) delegate to the vendor's own trainer via vendor_fit. Two families train on an objective that is neither:

  • Sundial trains its TimeFlow head — the checkpoint repo's own FlowLoss (velocity matching over patches), fed teacher-forced hidden states so that the state after patch i supervises patch i+1, which is what generate actually consumes. One thing has to be said plainly: the released checkpoint ships output_token_lens=[720], a generation setting — forward(labels=…) trims its labels to a length an input window never reaches, so the shipped 720-wide flow MLP cannot supervise a short window. Fine-tuning therefore rebuilds the flow head at the training patch length (re-initialised, ~11.4 M params) while the 12-layer trunk carries over. The trunk transfers; the head does not. That is a real limitation of the public checkpoint, not of the harness, and it is why prepare_training logs it.
  • t0 (α/β/γ) supervises the vendor's own differentiable pass: _single_pass is scaler.scale_input → forward → scaler.rescale_predictions, so its output is in data space and carries a graph, and forward is documented as "predict per-patch quantiles for every patch position (one differentiable pass)". The alignment is t0's own — _predict_step reads predictions[:, context_patches - 1], i.e. the patch after the last observed one — so the step scores the model on the steps that follow the context, with the future never fed. Its layers are named nothing like the usual ones (wQKV, wO, positional mlp.0/mlp.2), so the adapter declares lora_targets and head_prefixes=("head","decoder"); T0Forecaster is itself the nn.Module (there is no .model attribute, which is why this family used to report no trainable module).
  • Kairos uses the supervised forward's own loss, which comes back as one value per window; the trainer reduces it to its mean. (Before that reduction existed, the trainer's own if not torch.isfinite(loss) took the truthiness of the vector, and the resulting "Boolean value of Tensor with more than one value is ambiguous" was filed in the matrix as a Kairos limitation. It never was one.)

docs.title: What "not fine-tunable" means, honestly
docs.text:
Some families cannot be fine-tuned through an HF-style forward at all. They report — (skipped) with the reason, and it is a statement about the model:

  • TimesFM 2.0/2.5/3.0, TiRex, FlowState inference builds — no public training code; trainable() returns None, so the fine-tune column is —.
  • Kronos — the vendor loop only prepares the CSV unless extra={"run_training": True}; the matrix records prepared, not ok.
  • MOMENT — trainable, but its gradient checkpointing is non-deterministic, so the adapter disables it (otherwise torch aborts with "different number of tensors was saved").

docs.title: Three rows that used to be wrong in the other direction
docs.text:
The matrix refused Moirai 1.1, Moirai-MoE and Sundial fine-tunes for a while, and on inspection all three refusals were ours, not the models'. They are worth keeping in the docs because each is a trap that looks like a model limitation:

  • Moirai 1.1 / Moirai-MoE: reading quantiles off forward()'s samples gave a gradient-free "fine-tune", so the honest answer at the time was no differentiable head. The head is differentiable — it returns a distribution, and sampling is what predict does with it afterwards. The supervised step is uni2ts' own packed loss: MoiraiForecast._convert(patch_size, past…, future_target=truth…) → module → PackedNLLLoss over the prediction-masked patches, i.e. the objective the checkpoint was pretrained on. No dataset pipeline, no Lightning trainer, ~20 lines. One caution: MoiraiForecast.per_sample_loss_func is SampleNLLLoss (an evaluation loss); MoiraiFinetune's default is PackedNLLLoss. Both came back with the same number in testing, so don't assume the cheap one is a sampling estimator — check which tensor in the graph is stochastic before blaming the estimator for a noisy curve.
  • Sundial: the first attempt called forward(labels=…) with the checkpoint's own config and correctly reported "needs the vendor's training-script packing". What the vendor's fine-tune config actually does is choose the output token length for the run. Do that (rebuild flow_loss.FlowLoss at input_token_len) and the objective is theirs, the shapes are ours.
  • Kairos: see above — a scalar-reduction bug in our own trainer, mistaken for a gradient-unsafe vendor forward.

The lesson the ladder and the reason strings exist for: a fine-tune refusal must name the missing piece ("no target kwarg in forward", "labels trimmed to output_token_lens") so it can be checked rather than believed.

docs.title: The ladder: memory and numerics
docs.text: The fine-tune ladder walks keep → bf16 → fp16 → fp32 → lr×0.1 → ctx/2 → bs=1 → CPU. The first rungs are memory; the fp32 and lr×0.1 rungs are numerical, because a non-finite loss on step 1 is a property of that profile, not of the family (Toto-2.0-313m trains at a tenth of the fine-tuning rate). A run that fell off the ladder says which profile it actually trained on.

docs.title: Memory ladder
docs.text:
ForecastTrainer.fit (and RewardTrainer.fit) retry on OOM with progressively cheaper profiles, and record which one was used:

(bs, amp, peft) = (given) → (1, bf16, given) → (1, bf16, heads_only)
                          → (1, bf16, lora)  → (1, fp32, heads_only)

CUDA toolchain failures (nvrtc, arch mismatch) are treated the same way — a CPU retry is an environment fallback, not a silent downgrade; the checkpoint meta says fallbacks: [...].

docs.title: Checkpoints and provenance
docs.text:
from tsfm_trl import load_finetuned
from tsfm_trl.training.checkpoints import describe

describe("reports/ft/moirai-2.0-R-small__tiny_fin.pt")
m2 = ModelHub.load("moirai-2.0-R-small")
load_finetuned(m2, "reports/ft/moirai-2.0-R-small__tiny_fin.pt")

A checkpoint is a state dict plus the provenance needed to refuse a wrong pairing: base registry id, trainable parameter list, config, split index, loss curve, budget, smoke flag, and any fallbacks. load_finetuned raises if the target model's base id differs — a Chronos head loaded onto a Moirai is a silent nonsense machine otherwise. tsfm-trl ckpt <path> prints the same record.

docs.title: Vendor training loops have no curve at smoke size
docs.text: Two families fine-tune through the vendor's own loop (loss_kind = "vendor"): Chronos-2 (Chronos2Pipeline.fit, an HF Trainer) and Kronos (its finetune_csv). The adapter attaches a TrainerCallback so real runs surface their loss, but a vendor loop logs on its interval — at smoke size (a handful of steps) it never fires, so the matrix cell is a bare ✅ with no (a→b) pair. That is a logging gap in their loop, not a missing objective; the run's own stdout shows train_loss. Anything that must be compared side-by-side should be run with --budget fs64 or larger.

docs.title: 4 · Classification and probing
docs.text:
Three levels, from cheapest to most invasive. The plan requires all three to be checked for every model, and the matrix shows which one a family actually supports.

from tsfm_trl import ClassificationTrainer, ModelHub, TrainingConfig
from tsfm_trl.data.classify import direction_dataset, extreme_dataset, volreg_dataset, ucr_dataset

ds  = …                                   # a SeriesDataset (e.g. a price panel)
cds = direction_dataset(ds, horizon=5, ctx=120)
m   = ModelHub.load("moment-1-large", device="cuda")

ClassificationTrainer(m, TrainingConfig(budget="fs16"), route="probe").fit(cds)
ClassificationTrainer(m, TrainingConfig(budget="fs16", peft="lora"), route="head").fit(cds)
ClassificationTrainer(m, TrainingConfig(budget="fs16"), route="native").fit(cds)
route what trains notes probe nothing inside the model frozen representations + a classical classifier head a new readout head, optionally + lora on the trunk the default; unfreeze_trunk=True widens it native the family's own classification task/head only where the vendor provides one (MOMENT's classification task, Moirai's FORECASTING-style heads)

CLI:

tsfm-trl classify --model moment-1-large --task dir5 --levels probe,head,native

docs.title: Probe features
docs.text:
tsfm_trl.probing.features has two feature families, and the matrix reports them separately because a statistical probe is a baseline, not a property of the TSFM:

  • stat_matrix(X) — shape/scale-free summary statistics per window (level, trend slope, volatility, autocorrelation, crossing rate, tail statistics…). Any model, including none at all.
  • model_matrix(m, X) — the model's own embeddings/pooled hidden states, produced by m.embeddings(...) / m.classify_features(...). Models that expose no trunk representation decline with a CapabilityError, and the row shows —.

Both are evaluated with expanding-window CV (folds(cds.split, mode="expanding")): financial windows leak forward otherwise. The classifier is logistic or gradient boosting (make_classifier), and classify_eval(model, cds, routes=("probe_stat", "probe_model"), kinds=("logistic","gbm")) returns one row per combination.

docs.title: Label tasks
docs.text:
data.classify builds label sets from a SeriesDataset so a classification row means the same thing for every model:

builder task default direction_dataset(ds, horizon, ctx, band=0.25) sign of the forward move, with a dead-band (dir5-style 5-level variant via band) 2–5 classes extreme_dataset(ds, horizon, ctx, k=3.0) is the move beyond k conditional sigmas (*_extreme) 2 classes volreg_dataset(ds, horizon, ctx, n_bins=3) forward volatility regime 3 classes ucr_dataset(name, ctx) a tiny public UEA/UCR subset, for external validity per dataset

ClassificationDataset stores X (context arrays), y, and a time-ordered split (0 train / 1 test) — never a random split: shuffled windows across a price series are an information leak that makes every number in the table meaningless.

docs.title: What is refused
docs.text:
• Panel-only families (Kronos) cannot take plain 1-D contexts for a head; the row says — (needs OHLCV panels) — except Kronos, whose adapter writes the flat open=high=low=close, volume=amount=0 panel its own finetune_csv format uses, so its model-feature probe does run and says so in Pred.meta.
  • Models with no trunk output (TimesFM inference builds, TiRex) decline model_matrix with a CapabilityError; the statistical probe still runs, and the table labels it stat, so nobody mistakes it for a representation result.
  • classification_metrics reports balanced accuracy, macro-F1 and per-class counts — a 90 %-majority task that scores 90 % accuracy is visible as a 0.5 F1.

docs.title: 5 · Reward post-training (RewardTrainer)
docs.text:
One trainer, three mechanisms, chosen by what the model actually exposes:

mode what it optimises which families can do it grpo group-relative policy gradient on token log-probabilities token models: Chronos-T5, Time-MoE, Sundial (anything with loss_kind="token" + path_logprob) reward_descent direct gradient through a differentiable quantile head Chronos-2/Bolt, Moirai 2, Toto, TiRex-2, FlowState reward_descent_point same, on a mean-only head (interval terms switched off) MOMENT, small TTM releases rft rejection sampling / best-of-N: keep the best candidates, then supervise any family with a training_step 
from tsfm_trl import RewardSpec, RewardTrainer, ModelHub, TrainingConfig

m = ModelHub.load("chronos-2", device="cuda")
r = RewardTrainer(m, TrainingConfig(budget="fs16", steps=6, peft="heads_only"),
                  spec=RewardSpec(w_pinball=1.0, w_dir=0.5, w_cross=0.2),
                  n_candidates=8, kl=1e-3).fit(dataset)
r.extra["mode"]        # 'reward_descent'

CLI:

tsfm-trl reward --model chronos-t5 --steps 6 --candidates 8 --kl 1e-3 \
                --mode auto --budget fs16 --horizon 21 --ctx 256

docs.title: The default reward
docs.text:
RewardSpec is accuracy plus direction minus the pathologies that make a probabilistic forecast useless in a portfolio:

reward = −w_pinball · pinball(quantiles, truth)
         + w_dir     · directional_accuracy(median vs truth)
         − w_cross   · quantile-crossing penalty
reward clipped to ±spec.clip          # outlier windows must not dominate a batch

docs.title: Bring your own reward
docs.text:
Any callable with this signature replaces it — the trading case is the reason the signature has an anchor:

def pnl(candidates, truth, anchor, *, cost=2e-4):
    """candidates (B,K,H), truth (B,H), anchor (B,1) -> reward (B,K)

    anchor is the last observed price: P&L is relative, so a reward that ignores it
    silently rewards forecasts that are simply close to the mean of the context.
    """
    pos = np.sign(np.median(candidates, axis=2) - anchor)          # (B,K)
    ret = np.log(truth[:, -1:] / anchor) - np.log(truth[:, -1:] - 0 * anchor)
    return pos * np.sign(ret) - cost * (pos != 0)

RewardTrainer(m, cfg, reward=pnl).fit(ds)

docs.title: GRPO, concretely
docs.text:
Per step: draw K candidate continuations, score them, convert rewards to group-relative advantages A = (r − mean)/std across the group, then

loss = −Σ A · logp(candidates)  +  kl · KL(π ‖ π_ref)

with π_ref a frozen clone of the trainable parameters taken at the start of the run. That is the ordinary GRPO update, at smoke scale (reward_steps, n_candidates), which is what makes the matrix column meaningful: it proves the log-prob path, the candidate sampler and the KL anchor all run on that family.

docs.title: Honest limits
docs.text:
• This is reward post-training, not an RL benchmark. Six steps on 16 windows is a capability check; mean_reward in the output is the mean reward of the final step, not a policy's expected return.
  • reward_descent is not policy gradient — for a deterministic quantile head the reward is differentiable, and pretending otherwise would add variance for no bias-free benefit. The mode is recorded in the checkpoint and in TrainResult.extra["mode"].
  • Families with no gradient path at all (TimesFM inference builds, TiRex) report — (no reward path) rather than being run through a surrogate.
  • Moirai 1.1 / Moirai-MoE are —: their head draws samples, so a "reward gradient" would be noise with a learning rate attached.

docs.title: Memory
docs.text:
The same ladder as fine-tuning (bs/amp/peft stepped down on OOM), and the same rule that CUDA toolchain failures are environment problems: the run retries cheaper and writes fallbacks: [...] into the checkpoint, so a table never hides the fact that a row ran at bs=1 bf16 heads_only.

Runnable shape of the call: examples/04_reward.py (core env, one GPU, ~1 minute).

docs.title: Provenance: is this someone else's RL library?
docs.text:
No. RewardTrainer is hand-written in tsfm_trl/training/reward.py (~435 lines), and the dependency graph proves it: core dependencies are numpy/pandas/pyarrow/scikit-learn/scipy/pyyaml/tqdm, the [rl] extra is torch only, and nothing in the tree imports trl, trlx, verl, openrlhf or open_r1. The algorithm grpo refers to is Group Relative Policy Optimization (Shao et al. 2024, the DeepSeek-R1 recipe); the code here is our own minimal implementation of it.

What is faithful to GRPO

  • group-relative advantage, no value/critic network: adv = (r − r.mean(axis=group)) / (r.std(axis=group) + 1e-6);
  • K sampled continuations per window, scored by a reward that is not the loss;
  • a policy-gradient update on the model's own log-likelihood (Chronos adapter's path_logprob = sum of next-token log-probs from model(input_ids, labels=…)), so the objective is the model's own language, not a re-derived one.

What is deliberately simplified — say this out loud in any paper text:

  • only the max-advantage path per group gets the −A·logp term; standard GRPO averages the term over all K samples;
  • no PPO-style clipping and no π_old ratio — the update is the plain REINFORCE-with- group-baseline form;
  • the trust region is weight-space — a frozen clone of the trainable parameters taken at step 0, penalised as kl · Σ mean((p − p_ref)²) (kl defaults to 1e-3 in the class and 0.02 on the CLI) — not the paper's token-level KL to π_ref;
  • the reward is a forecast reward (scale-free accuracy + directional term + optional quantile-crossing penalty), not a program verifier.

So: GRPO-style is the accurate phrase; mode="grpo" in the matrix means "group-relative policy gradient over the model's own sampled token paths", and it is only reachable where an adapter exposes sample_paths + path_logprob — today the Chronos-T5 adapters (2 registered models). Kronos and Time-MoE expose sample_paths but no token log-prob, so they run rft, which is the group-baseline limit of the same objective and needs no likelihood.

Why not HuggingFace TRL's GRPOTrainer? It is bound to a causal-LM interface (logits → per-token log-probs, a Trainer training loop). Most TSFM architectures are not that: diffusion heads (Chronos-Bolt), masked-patch distribution heads (Moirai), quantile-regression heads (TTM, FlowState, Toto), flow-matching heads (Sundial, Aurora), RVQ tokens with a vendor training loop (Kronos). Adopting TRL would mean the RL half of the library only works for the two Chronos variants — and it would pin a Trainer dependency whose transitive requirements fight the per-family version pins that keep 11 environments working (docs/01_install.md).

To make it canonical (each step is small and localized):

  1. have path_logprob return the per-token sequence log-prob instead of the sum, and average the −A·logp term over all K candidates;
  2. snapshot π_old per iteration and add the clipped ratio;
  3. replace the weight-space anchor with a token-level KL against a frozen π_ref forward.

docs.title: Demonstrators (what was actually run)
docs.text:
Small data (16 windows, fs64 budget), one GPU. Every row is recorded with the quartile-mean comparison described above rather than first-step-vs-last-step, and with the parameter budget it actually trained — because a reward gain earned by 22 M free parameters and one earned by 0.3 M adapters are different claims.

model mode steps trainable reward early → late verdict chronos-t5-small grpo (8 sampled continuations, group-relative advantage) 96 1,081,344 (LoRA) 1.741 → 1.839 improved toto-2-22m rft (rejection-sampling filtered fine-tune) 48 295,296 (LoRA) −1.488 → −1.670 not improved toto-2-22m rft 48 21,915,584 (full) −1.488 → −1.669 not improved flowstate-r1 reward_descent 96 heads_only at bs=1 bf16 (ladder) −1.296 → −1.387 not improved

docs.title: Repeated runs: what a reward delta is worth
docs.text:
scripts/reward_seeds.py runs the same protocol over several seeds and reports the spread of the late-minus-early delta. Done properly (three seeds, and — for two of these — on two different machines), the picture is more interesting than the single-curve table above:

model mode configuration seeds late − early verdict chronos-t5-small grpo LoRA 1.08 M, lr 2e-5, bs 8, 96 steps 3 (A6000) +0.059 ± 0.013 3/3 improved flowstate-r1 reward_descent heads-only 1.18 M, lr 2e-5 (the configuration of the table above), bs 1, 96 steps 3 (GB10) + 3 (A6000) +0.136 ± 0.348 1/3 — sign not established flowstate-r1 reward_descent heads-only, lr 1e-4, bs 1, 96 steps 3 (GB10) + 3 (A6000) +0.426 ± 0.228 3/3 improved toto-2-22m rft LoRA 295 k, default lr, bs 4, 48 steps 3 (RTX Ada) −0.067 ± 0.109 1/3 — no effect at this budget

Three things follow, and they are the reason this section exists:

  • The FlowState row above ("not improved") was a single seed at lr 2e-5. Repeated at that configuration it is +0.136 ± 0.348 with 1/3 seeds improved — i.e. the original −0.09 sits comfortably inside its own noise. At lr 1e-4 the same model and mode improves 3/3 with a mean five times the size of the earlier point estimate. So the honest claim is not "reward descent does not work on FlowState" but "the reward trajectory at this budget is learning-rate sensitive, and a single seed at one learning rate supports no verdict in either direction."
  • The Toto negative result survives, with an error bar: −0.067 ± 0.109, 1/3 seeds. "RFT runs on Toto and does not improve reward at 48 steps" is supported; "RFT is useless for Toto" is not.
  • The harness is seed-deterministic across hardware. The lr-2e-5 FlowState runs on the aarch64 GB10 and the x86 A6000 agree to five decimals (+0.42577 vs +0.42576 for the lr-1e-4 pair). Seed-to-seed variation is enormous; machine-to-machine variation is not. So repeated runs must vary the seed, and cross-machine replication is a check on the environment, not a source of new variance.

A reproduction caveat worth recording: the original demo runs were done on the DGX, where the toto env now has a CPU-only torch (2.7.0+cpu) after its lock-file rebuild. A GPU-flagged reproduction there fails with Torch not compiled with CUDA enabled, which is environment drift, not a model result — the Toto seeds above were therefore run on the laptop GPU, and the sweep now records each env's torch build and CUDA availability per row (docs/08_known_issues.md).

The Toto row previously read −2.232 → −1.914, improved. It no longer does, and the reason is worth writing down rather than quietly fixing. Two things moved since that number was recorded: the reward's quantile-level grid (when the emitted head has a different number of levels than the caller asked for, the candidate grid is now the uniform one — the old scale is not comparable), and peft="lora" stopped training the trunk (docs/08_known_issues.md). Re-run at the current revision with both a 295 k adapter budget and the full 21.9 M-parameter model, the answer is the same in both cases: the reward drifts down. So RFT is a working path on Toto — the mode runs, the curve is logged, no fallback was needed — and a negative result at this budget.

The chronos-t5-small GRPO gain is the one positive claim here, and it survived the LoRA fix, which strengthens it: +0.10 reward from 1.08 M adapter parameters, no ladder fallback.

The FlowState row is kept as a negative result (re-run with quartile reporting: early mean −1.296, late mean −1.387). What it shows: the run fell to the ladder profile bs=1, amp=bf16, peft=heads_only under memory pressure, and gradient descent on the pinball-plus-direction reward at that profile drifts the reward down instead of up. A reward path is demonstrated (the mode runs, the curve is logged); a reward gain on a differentiable head is not demonstrated at this budget. Anyone concluding "reward post-training helps TSForecasters" from this repo would be over-reading it.

Reproduce:

tsfm-trl reward --model chronos-t5-small --steps 96 --bs 8 --lr 2e-5 \
                --budget fs64 --peft lora --device cuda
tsfm-trl reward --model toto-2-22m      --steps 48 --budget fs64 --peft lora --device cuda

docs.title: 6 · The compatibility matrix
docs.text:
tsfm-trl doctor --all-envs --md COMPATIBILITY.md --json reports/compat_matrix.json

One row per registry model, one column per capability. The point of the matrix is that it is produced by running, so it can be re-run by anyone on their own hardware and disagree with ours.

docs.title: What the table is for (and is not)
docs.text: This is an architecture-compatibility table, not a results table. Column order says so: the benchmark columns come first — load · forecast · quantiles · embed · classify · anomaly — then the two capability gates: reward (mode) and fine-tune (capability). A gate proves that a path exists and runs; it carries no accuracy claim. Effectiveness is measured by evaluate/forecast_eval and documented separately in docs/09_benchmark.md.

docs.title: How to read the symbols
docs.text:
symbol meaning ✅ it ran, and the output was checked (shapes finite, on the canonical grid, loss finite) ✅ grpo / rft / descent / descent·pt reward: which RL path the architecture allowed — token log-probs (grpo), sample-and-filter (rft), differentiable quantile head (descent), point head (descent·pt). The trainer chooses; see docs/05_reward_rl.md ✅ (0.587→0.612) fine-tune: first and last loss of the recorded curve. At matrix settings that is two smoke steps, so the pair proves the objective is differentiable and logging works — not that fine-tuning helps. A diverging run is still visible ✅ 2/2 classify: how many of the three levels (probe / head+LoRA / native) ran. native is only counted when the vendor ships a classification head at all, so MOMENT reads 3/3 and a quantile-head model 2/2 — the model/adapter declines this task, with a reason in the JSON (skipped) prepared a vendor loop was set up but not executed (vendor_fit paths, e.g. Chronos-T5's or Kronos' optional CSV script) ◐ partial: ran, but not fully verified or produced a degraded result ❌ it tried and failed; the captured reason is in the JSON · not checked in this run (--tasks subset)

skipped and failed are deliberately different: the first is a statement about the model, the second about the code or the machine. The weights column is separate from load, because "we have the weights" and "the model loads here" are different claims.

docs.title: What a row actually does
docs.text:
doctor.check(spec) runs, in order: load → predict (+ quantile-grid checks) → finetune → classify → anomaly → reward, each with its own try/except, and each recording a status and a reason string. Data comes from data.fixtures.tiny_finance (a synthetic regime-switching price series with an OHLCV panel) unless --series points at a real dataset.

Sizes are fixed and small on purpose:

--ctx 256 --horizon 16 --tasks ... --budget fs16 --steps 2 (smoke) --reward-steps 6

so a row costs seconds, not GPU-hours, and every model is measured at the same scale. --clf-windows 192 caps the classification set the same way (evenly spaced, splits proportional): a sampler model's classification features cost ~draws× more per window than a quantile head's, and an uncapped feature pass turned one Kronos row into an hour.

docs.title: Benchmark-shaped runs
docs.text:
If the question is "which architectures can I benchmark here", leave the two capability gates out and it is a few minutes per machine:

tsfm-trl doctor --all-envs --tasks load,predict,quantiles,embed,classify,anomaly \
                --ctx 512 --horizon 21 --json reports/matrix_bench.json

The reward pass is what fills the mode suffix in the reward column and the ## RL reachability table at the bottom of the markdown (which architecture exposes token log-probs, which only sample-and-filter, which have a differentiable head, and which vendor build simply ships no trainable path):

tsfm-trl doctor --all-envs --tasks reward --json reports/matrix_reward.json

Both write partial reports; merge them with the full one and the dedupe step keeps the task coverage the partial runs produced (a reward-only re-run does not erase a model's forecast column).

docs.title: Environment dispatch
docs.text:
--all-envs launches one subprocess per environment (envs/<name>/bin/python, plus anything mapped in envs/local.json), passing --env <name> so each env only checks its own rows. Reasons:

  • a segfault, OOM-kill or CUDA abort in one family cannot take the run down;
  • a family that needs transformers==4.40.2 and one that needs 4.57.6 both run in the interpreter they were verified in;
  • the JSON says which python and device produced each row.

An env that produces no JSON (argparse error, import crash, killed process) becomes a row of its own — <env tirex2> ❌ exit 1: … — instead of silently contributing nothing.

docs.title: Two machines, one table
docs.text:
--merge combines per-machine JSON reports. By default it keeps one row per (model, environment) — the row where the model actually ran — and writes the loser into the winner's reasons under other machine, so an aarch64-only Triton failure stays visible in an x86-clean table instead of vanishing. --keep-both opts out and prints one row per machine; the markdown adds a machine column whenever more than one machine contributed.

tsfm-trl doctor --merge reports/matrix_laptop.json reports/matrix_aarch64.json \
                --json reports/compat_matrix.json --md COMPATIBILITY.md

Useful flags:

tsfm-trl doctor --tier A --tasks load,predict --device cpu     # quick portability check
tsfm-trl doctor --model moment-1-large,moment-1-base --env moment
tsfm-trl doctor --merge reports/matrix_core.json reports/matrix_aarch64.json \
                --md COMPATIBILITY.md                          # combine per-machine runs

docs.title: Reproducing the published table
docs.text:
./scripts/make_envs.sh                                   # envs from envs/envs.toml
TSFM_WEIGHTS_ROOT=$HOME/models ./scripts/prefetch_weights.py --tier A
tsfm-trl doctor --all-envs --tasks load,predict,finetune,classify,anomaly,reward \
                --ctx 256 --horizon 16 --json reports/matrix_$(uname -m).json \
                --md reports/$(uname -m).md

Keep the JSON next to the markdown: the markdown shows the symbol, the JSON carries the reason string, and a table without reasons is decoration.

--md defaults to no file, not to COMPATIBILITY.md. A single-env run used to overwrite the merged table with its two rows; pass --md explicitly when that is what you want (the --merge invocation still defaults to COMPATIBILITY.md).

docs.title: 7 · Financial tasks, panels and leakage
docs.text: The label data here is finance-derived (plus a tiny public UEA/UCR subset for external validity), so the rules that keep the numbers meaningful are leakage rules.

docs.title: Dataset layout
docs.text:
A dataset directory is the most useful form because it carries the split you intend:

data/sp500_daily/
  meta.json          # {"name": "...", "target": "close", "freq": "1D"}
  train.parquet      # ┐ concatenated in this order; the split boundaries are
  validation.parquet   ├ preserved as index ranges, so an adapted model can be
  test.parquet       # ┘ proven never to have seen the evaluation span

A single .csv/.parquet works too (70/15/15 split), as does a DataFrame, a {train,validation,test}.npz, or a raw 1-D array.

The target column is meta.json["target"], else the first of close/target/y/value/price, else the last column.

docs.title: Panels and the price-column rule
docs.text:
SeriesDataset keeps the target as values and everything else as panel. Two rules that took a failed model run to learn:

  • panel_window(start, stop) re-attaches the target column. The panel excludes the target by construction, but a panel-consuming model (Kronos) asks for open/high/low/close and fails with Price columns ['open','high','low','close'] not found if close is missing from what it is handed.
  • A registry row declares what it needs in needs (e.g. ("close",)); rows with the panel_in capability get the DataFrame instead of a 1-D slice. A model that needs OHLCV cannot be fed a bare close series, and says so.

For fine-tuning, a panel-only vendor loop (Kronos' finetune_csv) synthesises the flat columns from the target and records that it did — a synthetic panel is disclosed in the checkpoint, not hidden.

docs.title: Label tasks
docs.text: dir/dir5 (direction with a dead band), extreme (move beyond k conditional sigmas), volreg (forward volatility regime) are defined in 04_classify_probing.md. All of them use rolling, backward-looking scale estimates: the band in dir5 is band × rolling-20-step log-return sd at the decision point, never the in-sample global sd. That is what lets one rule be applied to S&P and BTC without retuning.

docs.title: Splits and CV
docs.text:
• ClassificationDataset.split is time-ordered (0 train, 1 test). Shuffled windows over a price series leak the future into the training set.
  • Probes are evaluated with folds(split, mode="expanding"): each fold trains on the past and predicts the next block, like a backtest.
  • train_windows(..., split="train") records split_end_index (and the timestamp in split_end), and every checkpoint stores it. tsfm-trl ckpt <path> prints it, so an adapted model's evaluation can be audited for the leak before anyone believes its skill numbers.

docs.title: Anchor-relative metrics
docs.text:
On price panels, absolute MAE is dominated by the series' level and by volatility regimes, so the default comparisons are relative:

  • nd — normalised error against a naive anchor (last value);
  • mase — scaled by the in-sample naive error;
  • relative_skill(model_row, baseline_row) — versus a registered baseline (seasonal naive, theta, ARIMA), which is why baselines are first-class registry rows;
  • directional accuracy and rank_corr are reported per row, but only mean something next to the class base rate (a 60 % up-majority task makes 55 % accuracy worse).

The reward side of the library encodes the same idea structurally: the reward callable receives anchor (the last observed price) precisely so a P&L-style reward cannot be written to accidentally reward "forecast the context mean".

docs.title: What this library is not
docs.text: It is not a backtester: no costs, no position sizing, no portfolio accounting. The finance labels exist to give the models a hard, leakage-prone task at small scale. If you want tradable claims, bring your own walk-forward harness — and use the split_end provenance so it cannot overlap the training span.

docs.title: 8 · Known issues, pins and the reasons behind them
docs.text: Everything here was measured, not read. Where a family is broken, the entry says what the library does about it: fix, work around, or report honestly.

docs.title: The pins that decide whether a family runs
docs.text: family pin what happens if you ignore it Time-MoE transformers==4.40.2, numpy<2 4.42 introduced Cache objects → DynamicCache has no attribute from_legacy_cache; 4.44 removed standardize_cache_format → the released remote code dies. 4.38 is too old (EosTokenCriteria missing). Only 4.40.x works. TTM-r1 transformers==4.44.0 4.5x removed PatchTSMEncoderLayer. r2/r3 are fine on 4.57, which is why they live in core. Sundial transformers==4.42.4, numpy<2, einops==0.8.1 its repo code predates the 4.5x generation refactor. peft everywhere peft==0.19.1 0.20.x removed the base_model keyword our LoRA path passes. Toto safetensors==0.4.5 0.4.6 changed the deserializer its loader expects. TimesFM 2.0-500M timesfm==1.2.9 + jax (env timesfm20) PyPI's timesfm 2.0.x and 3.x are the 2.5/3.0 models; only 1.2.x still ships the v1 API (TimesFm, TimesFmHparams). 1.2.x imports jax at package import even for the torch backend. TiRex-2 Triton ≥ 3.4 and sm ≥ 10.0, else a CUDA toolchain (nvcc) Triton kernels die on older archs; the native fallback JIT-compiles a CUDA extension through flashrnn, so it needs nvcc — a runtime-only CUDA install (no toolchain) fails with Ninja is required…. On a laptop that is a machine gap, and TiRex2 raises UnavailableError naming both requirements rather than pretending the model is broken. datasets datasets>=3,<4 4.x needs an ABI-matched pyarrow.

docs.title: Model-level behaviour the adapters encode
docs.text:
• TimesFM 2.0-500M is 50 layers × 1280 dims × 16 heads. Building it with the 2.5 shape loads a state_dict with 700 "unexpected keys". A mismatch is reported as architecture, with the layer count, not a key dump. Forecast comes from TimesFm.forecast(inputs) -> (point, quantiles); there is no public training code, so fine-tune and reward are —.
  • Time-MoE's generate(do_sample=True) is broken in the released remote code (its prepare_inputs_for_generation hands transformers a 3-D tensor and _sample unpacks 2-D). Greedy works; sampling does not, in every transformers we tested. The adapter therefore does its own AR decode with a KV cache (_ar_decode), and the sampled paths are recorded in Pred.meta.
  • Time-MoE's forward mutates the tensor you pass it (in-place unsqueeze), so the decode loop clones on entry — otherwise the second step dies on a shape error that blames your own tensor.
  • Moirai 1.1 / Moirai-MoE cannot be fine-tuned through this API. Their forward() draws samples from the predicted distribution and _get_distr returns a distribution over the whole padded window, not the prediction slice: a gradient through "the quantiles of a sample" would be a no-op dressed as a fine-tune. The honest answer is skipped, with the reason, and the note that a real fine-tune needs uni2ts' own Lightning stack (MoiraiForecast + packed masked dataset). Moirai 2.0 exposes a differentiable quantile head → fine-tune ✅.
  • MOMENT fixes seq_len/pred_len at init(). Trainers call prepare_training(ctx, horizon) before asking for the module, and pipelines are cached per (task, horizon, seq_len) — rebuilding a 1 B backbone per call would dominate any fine-tune. MOMENT also turns gradient checkpointing on by default and its recomputation is not deterministic (different number of tensors was saved); the adapter disables it.
  • MOMENT has no quantile head (forward returns mean + samples), so reward post-training uses the reward_descent_point path (scale-free accuracy + direction), with the interval terms switched off rather than silently reported as zero.
  • FlowState/Granite: prediction_length = -1 in the config means flexible; the adapter discovers the real chunk length with one dry forward (_probe_head_len). Vendor models keep tensors in plain attributes, so LoRA/offload uses peft.move_deep to walk non-registered tensor buffers. CUDA toolchain failures (nvrtc, arch mismatch) are treated as environment, and the trainer retries on CPU.
  • Chronos-T5 tokenizes on CPU and moves the ids; label windows are truncated to config.prediction_length.
  • TiRex's loader validates a model id, not a path (Invalid model id when it is given a directory). ModelHub therefore passes source_id= (the registry id) to adapters so resolution to a local directory does not destroy the id.
  • Kronos needs an OHLCV panel, not a target series: SeriesDataset.panel_window re-attaches the target column (its close) because the panel drops it. A 1-D series is still accepted: the adapter writes the flat panel the vendor's own finetune_csv format uses (open = high = low = close, volume = amount = 0) — that is their convention for a single price series, not an invention here.
  • Kronos' predictor.predict returns a DataFrame of six OHLCV columns, averaged over its internal samples — so sample_count decodes happen and then the spread is thrown away. The adapter draws them itself through predict_batch (series × draws in one batched decode; 32 sequential calls turned a matrix run into an hour) and keeps Pred.samples, which is the only honest interval a sampler has.
  • Kronos fine-tunes in-process: training_step is the vendor's own next-token cross-entropy (frozen KronosTokenizer.encode → head.compute_loss), so LoRA, the memory ladder and the loss curve apply like every other family. vendor_fit still exports their CSV + config and prints the command for anyone who wants the script.
  • Kairos ships weights but no remote code (architectures: ["KairosModel"], no .py in the repo). It needs pip install git+https://github.com/foundation-model-research/Kairos which provides tsfm.model.kairos.AutoModel.
  • TTM r2/r3 declare no quantile levels. Their configs carry distribution_output=student_t and no quantiles list, so the head emits distribution parameters; inventing a 9-level grid from the parameter count would print an interval the model never predicted. _load_keep_info keeps the from_pretrained loading report, and where head tensors are newly initialised (ttm-r3 ships 80 of them that its released config does not describe) the adapter removes the quantiles capability and says why. Those rows are point-only, and reward post-training uses reward_descent_point.
  • f1_score does not take a beta. The recall-weighted F2 the finance framing needs lives in fbeta_score; passing beta= to f1_score raised and was swallowed by the except, so f1_beta2 was silently nan for every run. For >2 classes it is now the macro average of each occurring class's one-vs-rest F2.
  • PR-AUC and ROC-AUC need scores, not argmax. classification_report computes them one-vs-rest (weighted) when handed the score matrix, and reports nan — not a number — when the caller only has hard labels. All three classification routes now pass softmax scores.
  • A from-scratch head needs a from-scratch learning rate. The budget lr (1e-5) is a fine-tuning rate; at that step size a fresh MLP never leaves its initial bias, which reads as accuracy below chance. fit_head uses 1e-3 for the head with the trunk still on the fine-tuning rate (AdamW param groups).
  • stdout is a data channel. StepLog writes its JSON lines to stderr, and the per-env matrix children write their report to a temp file: a parent parsing a child's stdout for "the JSON" silently dropped every row once the step lines started sharing the stream.
  • statsmodels never shipped ThetaModel (absent in every release through 0.14/0.15, promised since 0.12). The theta baseline is implemented in-house (SES + drift).

docs.title: Design decisions that look like quirks
docs.text:
• CAPS is a frozenset — set(caps) <= CAPS in the registry tests is a subset check, and a tuple would make it silently wrong.
  • quantile_coverage reports only the bands a model actually emits. Reporting 95 % coverage for a model whose grid stops at 0.9 is an interval lie.
  • Pred.meta always says how an interval was produced (native head, empirical from n sampled paths, temperature-sampled AR decode, median-rollback rollout for horizons longer than one output patch).
  • skipped ≠ failed: — means the model/adapter declines the task (with a reason), ❌ means it tried and broke.
  • smoke counts as ok: the matrix checks that a capability runs, not that training converged. Loss curves are still printed (✅ (0.587→0.612)) so a fine-tune that diverges is visible.

docs.title: Vendor packages: the exact installs
docs.text:
These families publish no wheel on the index their model card names, and the matrix rows say which one is missing. On the laptop they live in .venv-vendor / .venv-toto (registered in envs/local.json):

family install import t0-α/β/γ pip install "tfc-t0[torch]>=0.6.1" from t0 import T0Forecaster (it is the nn.Module) Timestral 5/28/123/209M pip install git+https://github.com/mistralai/timestral.git from timestral import TimestralForecaster Hirondel-7M pip install git+https://github.com/tncrd/hirondel.git HirondelForecaster.from_pretrained(...).forecast([...]) Yug pip install yug from yug import YugPipeline Aurora pip install aurora-model from aurora import load_model Toto 2.0 pip install toto-models from toto2.model import Toto2Model Toto 1.0 pip install toto-ts (+ setuptools<81 for pkg_resources) from toto.model.toto import Toto
  • Vendor forecaster objects keep outputs on the GPU. np.asarray on a CUDA tensor raises can't convert cuda:0 device type tensor to numpy, which the matrix used to file as a failure of the model; base.to_numpy handles torch/jax/pandas.
  • Hirondel's forecaster is constructed from a model object, not a repo id: HirondelForecaster.from_pretrained(repo) then .forecast(list_of_contexts, prediction_length=) → .median (N,H), .quantiles (N,H,L), .quantile_levels.
  • Toto-Open-1.0 (toto-ts) is the one row still open. Its TotoForecaster takes the backbone (Toto(...).model) and a MaskedTimeseries(series, padding_mask, id_mask, timestamp_seconds, time_interval_seconds, num_exogenous_variables) built by their own dataset pipeline; the naive construction reaches einops shape errors. The adapter wiring is pending and the row reports that, rather than scoring an unverified path. Toto 2.0 (22m/313m) — the current generation — loads, forecasts, classifies and fine-tunes.
  • ~/.cache/huggingface/modules/transformers_modules owned by root (someone ran a pipeline as root on that box) makes every trust_remote_code model fail with PermissionError. Fix without sudo: export HF_MODULES_CACHE=$PWD/.cache/hf_modules.

docs.title: Numerical ladder
docs.text: A non-finite loss on step 1 is a property of that profile, not of the family. The fine-tune ladder now runs keep → bf16 → fp16 → fp32 → lr×0.1 → ctx/2 → bs=1 → CPU, and _is_unstable (nan/inf in the message) admits a run to the ladder instead of returning failed — which is how Toto-2.0-313m trains.

docs.title: Out of scope (and why)
docs.text:
• Moirai 2.0-R-base / -large: the repositories do not exist (404), gated or not.
  • Yug-1 (commercial): no weights. birlaailabs/yug (CC-BY-NC) is registered instead, with the license recorded in the row.
  • VisionTS++ / t0-α/β/γ base weights: the authors host them outside the Hub; the rows carry weights: null plus a pointer instead of pretending they are fetchable.
  • Any model whose weights require a login we do not have.

docs.title: Second pass: per-machine matrix, three classify levels
docs.text:
The matrix is now run on two machines (x86 laptop, RTX 1000 Ada 6 GB; aarch64 DGX Spark, GB10 unified memory) and merged. What that surfaced:

  • One row per (model, env), the working row wins. When the two machines disagree — TiRex-2 compiles on sm8.9 but its Triton kernel raises CompilationError on the GB10; MOMENT-large fine-tunes on 6 GB fp16 but OOMs then recovers on unified memory — dedupe() keeps the row that ran and records the other machine's reason under other machine:, so a failure never disappears, it moves to a footnote. --keep-both opts out. A row whose env no longer matches the registry is dropped at merge time: the model moved environments, and listing it twice double-counts it.
  • Machine gap ≠ model failure. UnavailableError: needs Triton and an sm10.0+ GPU, or nvcc for the MLSTM fallback is an environment statement. The same model is ✅ on the other machine. The matrix prints both columns; the prose in this file is where the difference is explained.
  • trust_remote_code on a shared box: HF_MODULES_CACHE must point somewhere writable, or every custom-code model (Chronos-Bolt variants, VisionTS, Sundial, Kairos) fails identically at import time.
  • Vendor envs are architecture-specific. A freeze.txt generated on x86_64 cannot be installed on aarch64. On the DGX the Toto env had to be rebuilt from the local core freeze plus the Toto delta (transformers==5.10.1, safetensors==0.4.5, tokenizers==0.22.2, torchmetrics, setuptools<81); with the frozen x86 file it silently ends up without transformers at all and every row says missing package.
  • TimesFM 2.0/2.5 are v1-API models (timesfm==1.2.9 + JAX). The PyPI package's 2.x and 3.x lines are different checkpoints with a different API; the adapter pins the arch dict (num_layers=50, num_heads=16, model_dims=1280, input_patch_len=32, output_patch_len=128) because the config in the repo doesn't carry it.
  • Aurora's load_model() returns a model in train mode, so its norm layers raise Expected more than 1 value per channel on the batch of one that inference is made of; the adapter calls .eval(). Its flow-matching head has no public training path, so fine-tune and reward report —, not ❌.
  • Hirondel fine-tunes in its own normalised space. HirondelModel.forward(x, observed, horizon) returns quantiles after mean/sd + asinh scaling; the adapter's training_step applies _scale to the context and the same transform to the target before the pinball loss, so the optimised objective is the one the forecaster inverts. Reward runs as rft (its head is not a differentiable quantile head in the sense reward_descent needs).
  • Kairos emits 128 steps for a 16-step request (its prediction_length is fixed by the checkpoint). The adapter slices; fine-tune remains open because the vendor forward branches on tensor truthiness — reported as ❌ Boolean value of Tensor ..., not hidden.
  • MOMENT's native classification head takes num_class (not n_class), and its pipeline forward is keyword-only (x_enc=). Both appear in fit_native, which now tries positional then keyword. The pipeline object is cached: calling pipeline() per step re-downloads.
  • Reward: --steps beats reward_steps. reward_steps is the matrix cap (a reward row checks that post-training runs, in seconds). Silently trimming a requested 48-step demonstrator to 6 was how a run "did not improve". The cap now applies only when no step count was given.
  • Reward trend is reported by quartile means (reward_early_mean vs reward_late_mean), not first step vs last step. First-vs-last called a run that improved (1.72 → 1.83 across quartiles) a regression, because step 1 happened to be a lucky batch.

docs.title: Third pass: Sundial, Toto 1.0, and what a moving repository does to a matrix
docs.text:
• Sundial's Hub repo changed under us. The current revision has no prepare_input_ids, ships no tokenizer files, and its model card's Quickstart is the truth: model.generate(torch.randn(B, lookback), max_new_tokens=H, num_samples=k) → (B, k, H) de-normalised samples (the mixin does revin itself). The older prepare_input_ids(X=…, system="forecast") + tokenizer= call is still in a lot of second-hand examples and no longer exists; the adapter prefers whichever API the loaded code provides. Two version facts, both verified on the matrix machine: transformers==4.40.1 is required (4.42.x mis-builds the causal mask for patched inputs and generate dies with a 256-vs-16 shape error), and device_map= must not be passed to this remote code (accelerate re-dispatches through the Auto mapping, which does not know model_type: sundial, and raises "Unrecognized configuration class").
  • Sundial fine-tune is declined, not failed. forward(labels=…) reaches their TimeFlow loss, whose packing (output_token_lens, diffusion_batch_mul, mask_y) is set by the training scripts rather than the checkpoint config. Calling it with the checkpoint's own config fails on shape (addmm: (8x17664) @ (768x768)). Writing an invented objective to turn that row green is exactly what this repository is not for, so the row says — and points at thuml/Sundial's scripts/.
  • Toto-Open-1.0 does not go through transformers at all — the repo has no remote code and no model_type, so the Auto path raises "Should have a model_type key". The vendor package toto-ts is the implementation: Toto.from_pretrained(repo, map_location=...) (a ModelHubMixin loader — no device_map/dtype kwargs, they get forwarded into the model config and crash the constructor), then TotoForecaster(model=model.model) — it wants the backbone — and a MaskedTimeseries built exactly like their own evaluation/fev pipeline (relative timestamps, time_interval_seconds=1, id_mask ones). num_samples must be divisible by samples_per_batch; intervals are empirical quantiles of the sampled paths and Pred.meta says so. Fine-tune uses their CombinedLoss (NLL + general robust loss) on the causally-scaled window, which is the pretraining objective.
  • PatchTST-FM (tsfm_public) declares no target argument in the installed build (forward(past_values, past_observed_mask, pad_mask, prediction_length, quantile_levels, return_loss)), so a fine-tune that passed future_values= used to be a TypeError. The adapter now picks the target kwarg from the signature and, when there is none, declines with the signature in the reason. Its head is backbone.out_layer, so head_prefixes had to be declared — heads_only (the reward ladder profile) was failing with "matched no parameters" against generic prefixes.
  • TiRex-2 fails on both machines, for different reasons, and the matrix says so: x86 (sm8.9, no nvcc) → neither Triton nor the CUDA fallback is available (UnavailableError); aarch64 GB10 → Triton starts compiling their recurrent kernel and raises CompilationError inside it. It is the only registered model that does not forecast anywhere here, and it stays ❌ rather than being dropped from the table.
  • tsfm_trl now fixes the HF dynamic-module cache at import if ~/.cache/huggingface/modules is not writable (someone ran a pipeline as root on the box). Without it, every trust_remote_code model fails with PermissionError, which a compatibility matrix would file as 6 model failures. The redirect prints one line to stderr rather than happening silently.

docs.title: Fourth pass: three fine-tune refusals that turned out to be ours
docs.text:
The fine-tune column carried — for Moirai 1.1/MoE and Sundial, and ❌ for Kairos. All three were harness bugs wearing a model's face; each is now ✅, and the fix in each case was to stop inventing a step and go read what the vendor's own training does.

  • Moirai 1.1 / MoE — forward() returns a distribution; predict samples from it. Because the sampled path is gradient-free, the adapter declared "no differentiable head". The supervised step was in the same class the whole time: MoiraiForecast builds packed fields (target/observed_mask/sample_id/time_id/variate_id/prediction_mask) and scores them with PackedNLLLoss — uni2ts' own MoiraiFinetune default. The adapter now calls _convert(...) with the true future as future_target and optimises that. Trainable: 4.1 M (heads_only) / 5.9 M (LoRA) on moirai-1.1-R-small, 13.5 M on the base, 7.2 M on MoE. loss: vendor in the registry now says what the objective is.
  • Sundial — supervised forward(labels=…) with the shipped config fails on shape because output_token_lens=[720] is a generation setting: labels get trimmed to seq_len − input_token_len + 720, a length a short window never reaches. Their fine-tune config sets the output token length per run; prepare_training now does the same and rebuilds flow_loss.FlowLoss(16, 768, 3, 768, 50) at input_token_len. Cost, stated in the adapter docstring: that head is re-initialised (11.4 M params), the 12-layer trunk transfers. Frozen trunk + new head on 12 steps: 3.77 → 0.25. peft.lora_trains_head exists for exactly this case — a rebuilt head has no pretrained weights for LoRA to nudge, so it trains outright next to the trunk adapters.
  • Kairos — RuntimeError: Boolean value of Tensor with more than one value is ambiguous looked like a gradient-unsafe vendor forward. It was our own if not torch.isfinite(loss) running on the per-window loss vector their supervised forward returns. The trainer now reduces non-scalar losses to their mean (and says so in the run notes); 10 M/50 M train at 2.97 M / 7.17 M LoRA parameters.

One more honesty note that came out of this pass: the loss curve of a 2-step smoke says nothing — smoke=True caps the run at two steps, and Moirai's packed NLL swings ±0.9 between random batches. The matrix ✅ means "a differentiable vendor objective ran and logged"; direction needs ≥20 steps (docs/03_fine_tune.md).

docs.title: peft="lora" used to include the trunk
docs.text:
Worth its own heading because it inflates every LoRA number recorded before the fix: apply_lora._inject froze the nn.Linears it wrapped and enabled their adapters, but froze nothing else, and HF models load with requires_grad=True. make_trainable now freezes all parameters before injecting, then re-enables the adapters (and, for adapters that re-initialise a head — lora_trains_head, used by Sundial — that head). Two symptoms that were easy to misread as model behaviour: t0-gamma's 156 M "trainable" parameters, and a t0 LoRA loss that rose from 2.2 to 6.0 in two steps because the trunk was being moved at the fine-tuning rate.

Related: the lora_trains_head branch called a helper that did not exist (_matches_any instead of _match), which is a NameError waiting inside a path only Sundial takes. ruff check tsfm_trl --select F,E9 catches it; check.sh runs that before the matrix, which is exactly why check.sh exists.

docs.title: Fifth pass: two dead CLI paths, and Chronos-2's output-patch cap
docs.text:
• tsfm-trl evaluate and tsfm-trl info were both broken and untested. evaluate called _load_model(a.model) where the function wants the whole namespace ('str' object has no attribute 'model'); info printed s.note while the registry field is notes. Neither path is used by the matrix or the examples, so 32 green tests said nothing about them. tests/test_cli.py now drives the CLI surface on the statistical baselines — no weights, no GPU, two seconds — which is exactly the layer that had no coverage.
  • Chronos-2's supervised forward is capped by num_output_patches, default 1. The adapter called model(context=…, future_target=…) without it, so any horizon above one output patch (16 steps) died in _validate_input, and the channels-last retry below it turned that into the still more misleading context must have shape (batch_size, context_length). The vendor derives the argument from the prediction length; the adapter does the same now (ceil(H / output_patch_size)), so fine-tune/reward work at 16/21/64. Nothing about the checkpoint is rebuilt — the output embedding is applied per patch.
  • A fallback must not eat the original error. That row's captured reason was the retry's message, which named neither the argument nor the cap. The retry now re-raises the first exception.
  • TSFMTRL_DEBUG=1 prints the traceback of anything the matrix swallows, from the row capture and from every rung of the reward-mode ladder. The report keeps only messages (one bad model must not end a 46-model run), which is right for the table and useless for fixing a failure that only appears inside the matrix. It goes to stderr; stdout stays the data channel.
  • Vendor loops log on their own interval. A Chronos-2/Kronos vendor fine-tune at smoke size produces no loss pair in the matrix cell; recorded rather than hidden (docs/03_fine_tune.md).

docs.title: Normalising an interpreter path can leave the venv
docs.text: Recording which interpreter produced a row means storing its path, and the obvious Path(py).resolve() is a trap: env/bin/python is a symlink to the base interpreter that built the venv, so resolve() hands back something under uv's python directory with none of the family's pinned packages. The run then dies on import numpy in 0.0 s and the failure looks like a broken model environment. scripts/sweep_evaluate.py uses os.path.abspath() (lexical, no symlink following) and tests/test_sweep_paths.py keeps that true — the same distinction that makes sys.executable and realpath(sys.executable) different tools.

docs.title: A family env can silently lose its GPU
docs.text:
Lock-file rebuilds on aarch64 resolved CPU wheels in three of the twelve DGX environments (toto → torch 2.7.0+cpu, timesfm20 and new → torch 2.8.0+cpu). Nothing about the run looked wrong: --device auto quietly chose CPU, the numbers came out plausible, and a run that asked for CUDA failed with Torch not compiled with CUDA enabled — which reads like a model or harness failure and is neither. Two mitigations are now in the tooling:

  • the sweep probes each env's interpreter once (torch.__version__, torch.cuda.is_available(), device name), prints a NOTE when --device cuda was asked for and the env has no CUDA, and writes the probe into every record and into the report's provenance table;
  • the reward seeding script does the same for the child interpreter before spending minutes on a doomed run.

The lesson generalises: a benchmark row is its environment. A CPU row and a GPU row for the same model are different experiments, and "it ran" is not evidence about which one you got.

docs.title: Seventh pass: 101 series, and three ways a number can be wrong without any code erroring
A checkpoint's context length is an interface, not a suggestion
docs.text:
granite-timeseries-ttm-r3 declares context_length = 512. Fed the protocol window of 256 it pads its own input with zeros, and the whole forecast comes back scaled by the fraction of real history: measured on one equity series, the mean prediction is 0.25x the context at ctx 128, 0.50x at ctx 256, 0.99x at 512. In the first pass-3 ranking that read as "median MASE 13x naive, 0% of series beaten" for a model whose weights are fine. The artifact was our window.

Fix: TSFMModel.min_context (read by the Granite adapter from the checkpoint config). forecast_eval raises the benchmark context to it when the span allows and writes context raised 256->512 (checkpoint contract) into the row's ctx_note; when the span cannot supply it the adapter pads on the left with the oldest observation instead of letting vendor code feed zeros, and says so in Pred.meta. The row's ctx column then shows 512 for those models, which is why the effectiveness table has a ctx column per row at all.

The honest residual: with the contract honoured, TTM r2 behaves normally (MASE ~3-9) and r3 still loses badly on financial series because its forecast is nearly flat (std ~0.8 against a truth std ~8 on a volatile equity) - an approximate mean-forecaster on low-volatility price data. Finding and artifact are now separable; before, they were the same number.

min_context is set only where the padding artifact was measured. A contract probe over the sweep models (one equity series, level ratio at ctx 256 versus the declared length) found FlowState declaring 2048 and PatchTST-FM 8192 while both score normally at 256 - FlowState actually gets worse at its declared length (level ratio 0.587 at 2048 against 1.135 at 256). Those models accept short windows honestly, so raising their context would change the experiment rather than repair it. The rule is: measure the padding behavior, then declare the contract - do not read a config number and treat it as a requirement.

docs.title: NaN is a failed measurement, not a metric value
docs.text:
TTM r3 also emits an all-NaN point head intermittently: the same 512-point window was clean in one process and NaN in the next. Two wrongs were hiding in the old path: the vendor model returned NaN without raising, and forecast_report is nan-safe, so it scored the surviving 3 of 4 windows while the row still claimed n_windows: 4. My own ranking script then aggregated a column containing NaN and printed "median MASE nan" for the model - which looks like a joke and reads like one.

Now: retry each affected window alone (a batch can poison a model's own per-instance normalisation), drop whatever is still non-finite from the scoring set, record pred_nan_windows plus an error string, set n_windows to the number actually scored, and emit None rather than NaN in metric columns.

docs.title: Report sections that iterate the wrong collection under-count across lanes
docs.text: report() merges cells per (model, series, span, horizon) but keeps one raw record per model in rec_by_model. The tables read the merged cells; the "Not scoreable on some series" section and the new untrained-head section read recs. With two GPU lanes each carrying half the corpus, the flag list showed 33 of 66 flagged MOMENT series, and the covariate-panel section was under-counted in pass 2 the same way. Both now read the merged rows, and a model that scored anywhere is no longer listed as dataset-unscoreable. Symptom to remember: a summary section whose count is exactly one lane's worth.

docs.title: Shared cards: free at launch is not free during
docs.text: chronos-t5-base lost 33 of 66 series to torch.OutOfMemoryError with the error reporting 44.94 MiB free, minutes after nvidia-smi showed ~10 GiB - another user's process grew to 26 GiB mid-run, and our own peak was 7.09 GiB. The lane runner's --min-free-mib guard is necessary, not sufficient. Two operational rules follow: pin CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES to the index you chose (a retry that picked "cuda" from a free-memory total landed on the contended GPU 0 anyway), and treat a mid-run OOM as an environment event to re-run, never as a model result. Where the cards stay full, the retry runs on CPU lanes and the rows carry device: cpu.

docs.title: Two small tooling facts from this pass
docs.text:
• --md path/to/report.md now creates the parent directory; before, the first invocation into a fresh run directory died on FileNotFoundError after doing all the merge work.
  • The trux core env has no ruff, so scripts/check.sh stops at the lint stage there. Tests, registry consistency and the mini matrix are run on trux; lint stays a laptop gate. That is a real gap in the multi-machine story, not a covered one.

docs.title: Syncing a checkout with rsync --delete deletes the environments living inside it
docs.text:
The harness exists twice on the laptop: the standalone repo and trl/ in this checkout, which is what the other machines fetch. Bringing the standalone repo up to date with rsync -a --delete overwrote more than the code. Two things were gone before I looked at the file list:

  • .github/workflows/docs.yml — this tree has no .github/, so --delete removed the Pages build. Nothing in the harness test suite notices a missing CI file.
  • Every family venv under envs/ (several GB, built over days) — same reason: they are in the destination and not in the source. The locks and envs.toml survived, so the fix is scripts/make_envs.sh, not an archaeology hunt, but the run I was mid-way through on the laptop was over.

Nothing tracked by git was lost (git status showed 89 modified/added paths, 0 deletions), which is the only reason this was an afternoon and not a data-loss incident.
