The rule now: when one checkout feeds another, list what may move (git ls-files, plus the probe and report text manifests) and copy that, or keep --delete off and let git show what is missing. A working tree that holds installed environments is never a safe rsync target.

Because the two checkouts drift, the standalone repo is now pushed (master @ the sync commit, plus a pre-sync-2026-11-26 branch holding the state before it), and this tree stays the source the machines clone. Docs edits are meant to land in both; where they haven't yet, this file is the one to trust.

docs.title: A row's model field is the adapter's family key, and ten checkpoints collide on it
docs.text:
The registry key (chronos-bolt-small) is not what lands in a result row. The adapter writes its family key (chronos-bolt), so one row-level id can come from several checkpoints. Across the registry there are ten such collisions:

chronos-bolt   <- chronos-bolt-small, chronos-bolt-base
chronos-t5     <- chronos-t5-small,   chronos-t5-base
ttm-r2         <- ttm-r2,             ttm-r3
kronos-small   <- kronos-small,       kronos-base,  kronos-mini
moment-1-large <- moment-1-small,     moment-1-large
moirai-1.1, toto-2-22m, kairos-10m, ... (same pattern)

The report was safe (it keys merges on the record-level registry key and stamps model_key when reading), but nothing said that out loud, and my own comparison script keyed on the row field. The result was a fabricated finding: "chronos-bolt disagrees by 3-40% between the pass-3 run and today's re-run" — which was really bolt-small vs bolt-base being averaged together, and it nearly sent me chasing cuBLAS nondeterminism across GPU generations. After the fix, GB10 (gpu7) and RTX 6000 Ada agree bit-exactly (0.000%) on every overlapping cell, baselines and neural models alike.

Two changes: every written row now carries model_key (stamp_rows), and the merge keeps its model_key stamp on read for older files. probes/trux/cross_machine_check.py keys on the registry key for the same reason. The trap generalises: a label chosen by the code under test is not an identifier for the analysis on top of it.

Follow-up, because the first reading of the duplicates was also wrong. With the key fixed, the merge's 404 repeated cell keys were re-scored by protocol signature (ctx, ctx_note, device, code_sha, torch). They are overwhelmingly supersessions: a TTM cell measured at ctx 256 (MASE 30.1, the zero-padding artifact) and the same cell at its contract ctx 512 (MASE 4.3). Only repeats with an identical signature can be read as run variance, and once separated they are small: 254 repeated comparisons on trux - pass-3 lanes at sha 1d2f3ae against re-runs at 28fd7e7 - agree to 0.143%, and the DGX Spark matches trux to 0.000%. So the journal's earlier "neural cells vary 2-200% run to run" was one artifact (the collided key) compounding another (a fixed protocol change counted as noise). Reproducibility in this benchmark is now measured, not assumed, and the report section says which of the two a repeated key is before it quotes a number.

docs.title: A GPU that answers [N/A] for memory is a scheduler bug waiting to happen
docs.text: The DGX Spark (GB10, aarch64, unified memory) reports memory.free and memory.total as [N/A] while torch.cuda.is_available() is true and the device works. The lane scheduler parsed those rows away, so gpu_free() returned an empty pool and every lane fell back to CPU on a machine with a working GPU — the row would still have been written, just labelled device: cpu, which is how a new arm of the benchmark would have produced a table of CPU numbers under a GPU heading. parse_gpu_rows now drops only non-numeric memory rows and tolerates extra trailing columns; gpu_free() falls back to torch.cuda.mem_get_info() and tags the row reported_by: torch, because a number used for scheduling should say where it came from. Two facts to keep straight: nvidia-smi knowing the GPU exists is not the same as knowing its free memory, and strict unpacking of a tool's csv turns a column change into silently empty output.

docs.title: Sixth pass: moving the harness onto other machines
docs.text:
The same code went to trux (2× RTX 6000 Ada) and watson (SLURM, A6000). What broke was not the models; it was the boundary between "a machine that has this project" and "a machine that has the right environments".

A recorded skip is sticky. On watson the first run had no envs/local.json, so all 16 models were written as env-skips — the resolver refusing to run a family in a foreign interpreter, exactly as designed. After writing the mapping, the next run printed 0 ok / 0 failed / 0 env-skipped, which reads like a working sweep: the models already appear in the incremental JSONL, so resume treats them as done. Fixing the environment is not enough — the log needs --fresh. The merge rule ("rows beat errors") hides the symptom in a report, not the trap at launch.

Seven of twelve lock files do not re-resolve (core, moment, new, timemoe, tirex2, toto, ttm): uv proves the frozen set contradicts itself, e.g. gluonts wants pandas<2.2 while the freeze pins 2.3.3. Those freezes were taken from layered installs, so they are a record of what worked, not a recipe a solver can reproduce. uv pip install --no-deps -r <lock> reinstalls exactly the recorded set; a solver-driven install does not. core.lock.txt also carries no torch pin by design (torch is platform-specific and installed separately), which surprises anyone expecting one command to rebuild an env. Related drift: envs.toml notes transformers==4.57.6 for core while the committed lock pins 5.22.1 — the lock records a later, drifted env, not the one that produced the published matrix.

A plausible command line is not the real one. The lane runner had been written against a remembered CLI: --windows and positional series do not exist (--max-windows, repeatable --series). It died at launch, which is the cheap way to find out. Now probes/trux/selftest/ keeps a stub whose argparse mirrors sweep_evaluate.py --help, so an interface drift fails a 1-second test instead of a 12-hour sweep. Note that the real CLI inherits argparse prefix matching, so a typo like --windows=3 is silently accepted as --max-windows=3; the stub forbids abbreviations so a runner cannot lean on that hazard.

Flattening the corpus needs a rule, not a shrug. The corpus stores parquet splits, the sweep documents timestamp,close CSVs. Flattening found 19 series whose splits share timestamps — always across splits, never within one, which is lookback context reuse. But open/sp500_daily's train range runs past its validation range, with validation entirely inside train. Zero-shot rows sliding over the whole series are unaffected; calling those splits held-out data is wrong. The converter now records overlap kind and range per series, and refuses to flatten a timestamp that carries different values.

A green cell can still be an untrained head. MOMENT's released checkpoint contains one head — head.linear (8, d_model), reconstruction. Asking for task_name="forecasting" loads that head unchanged (transformers reports "0 missing keys" because the new head has different shapes), and the init() the model card tells you to call replaces it with a randomly initialised one. The compatibility matrix therefore shows a pass; the benchmark rows say what ran — MASE 7.0–19.6 where a naive forecast gets 2.1–8.4, large within ~1 of small. Rows now carry head_from_checkpoint and head_trained_here, and the report lists flagged models under "Flagged: the scored head was never trained" while keeping the numbers.

docs.title: Fine-tune pass: the lr moved the number, and the job script lost its own summary
docs.text:
MOMENT is now the only family with both zero-shot and fine-tuned cells on the same series (12 series, A6000, reports/moment_ft_watson/lane_ft.jsonl). Two findings:

Learning rate dominated the adaptation scope. At lr 1e-6, training only the head left the score where zero-shot left it (2.42x naive vs 2.56x); at lr 1e-4 with only the head trainable it reached 1.67x, matching a full fine-tune of the whole model. Sweeping heads_only vs full while leaving lr at a default compares two things when one knob matters. --configs therefore accepts peft:budget[:lr] and the sweep records lr per run, so a null result can be attributed instead of being read as a property of the family.

A batch job can succeed and still print nothing useful. The MOMENT job finished — 2373 s, 156 run records, done in 2373s -> reports/moment_ft_watson/lane_ft.jsonl — and then its trailing summary line failed with envs/core/bin/python: No such file or directory, because the script used a path relative to a directory SLURM had not made the cwd. The results survived only because the lane file is written as it goes; a harness that emits its numbers at the end of the script would have produced a successful-looking job with no data. Job scripts should use absolute paths for their own environment, and the lane file should be append-as-you-go (it is).

docs.title: A dispatched bridge job is one file: three failures, one rule
docs.text:
Getting the GB10 replication job to run took four attempts, and all three failures were the same fact approached from a different angle: trux_dispatch.sh transfers one file to the worker's inbox, and the worker runs it in a fresh shell on the far machine.

attempt what was assumed what happened job_006 SERIES_LIST=... bash trux_dispatch.sh job.sh would carry the argument FATAL: SERIES_LIST required - the env never crosses job_007 the job may read a sibling file (gpu7_watson12.series) "next to the script" cat: .../inbox/gpu7_watson12.series: No such file - only the job file lands there job_008 the job may exec the real runner from the repo clone by relative path bash: .../inbox/gpu7_030_replicate.sh: No such file - $0 is in the inbox, not the repo

The job that works (job_009+) is generated: the runner body plus the series list inlined. Two side lessons from the same loop. The generated file had a literal \n spliced into a line continuation, which bash read as the word n passed to git pull, so the repo never advanced and the failure surfaced as a WARN - a generator that concatenates strings needs the same lint as hand-written code. And --models chronos2 died with unknown model(s): the registry key is chronos-2 while the family is chronos2; the sweep validating model names at startup, rather than defaulting to a substring match, is what made that a five-second failure instead of a silently empty lane.

docs.title: The same series name can be two different measurements: CSV vs arena directory
docs.text:
The GB10 replication lane was the first real overlap between machines: 12 series watson had already scored, 216 shared cells. probes/trux/cross_machine_check.py called 212 of them disagreements, with MASE off by 14.98%, 37.68%, 30.80% — up to 122.9%. None of it was hardware. The signature of the bug was in what agreed: RMSE matched to about the eighth decimal, directional accuracy was identical, and both horizons of one series were off by exactly the same ratio.

mase(y, p, train) is mean|y-p| / mean|diff(train)|. The numerator is the forecast; the denominator is a property of which split the loader invented. trux and gpu7 read the arena directory std_equity_1d_10104 (publisher's train/validation/test parquets, train n=1510, naive MAE 0.375671). Watson's pass-3 job read ~/pass3_csv/std_equity_1d_10104.csv, a flat file, so SeriesDataset synthesized a 70/15/15 split (train n=1937, naive MAE 0.431936). Their ratio is 0.8697; its reciprocal 1.1498 is the observed MASE ratio for that series to four decimals. The forecasts were the same numbers.

What that does to the published table:

  • Survives: beats naive per cell (the naive baseline in the same lane shares the denominator), and the unscaled metrics — rmse, mae, dir_acc. Cross-machine on those: bit-exact.
  • Does not survive: any absolute MASE comparison between the watson block (35 series, CSV) and the trux block (66 series, arena dirs). They are two scales of the same quantity, differing per series by 1.0x–2.2x depending on where the publisher's train boundary sits relative to 70%.

The fix is a fingerprint, not a rule to remember. SeriesDataset now stamps data_hash — sha1 over the loaded values and the split boundaries, 12 hex chars — and data_kind (arena_dir / csv / parquet_file / in-memory / frame) into meta, and forecast_eval copies both onto every scored row. scripts/sweep_evaluate.py adds the lane meta field data_kinds, and both consumers use it: the merge's protocol signature includes the data path, so a CSV/arena repeat of one cell is filed under superseded rather than run variance; cross_machine_check.py refuses to call it a machine disagreement and exits 2 (inconclusive), with a fallback for legacy lanes that predate the row-level stamp — their meta line still lists the input names, and .csv versus a bare directory name is enough to tell which split was loaded.

The general form: a series name identifies a file, not a measurement. Anything scaled by a quantity derived from the data (MASE by the train-split naive error, any z-scored metric, any "beat baseline by X%" claim) silently changes when the data path changes, and the only durable defence is to write down the bytes and the split next to the number.

docs.title: --device is a record, not a constraint - until the adapter enforces it
docs.text:
A trux lane run with --device cpu wrote device: cpu into its meta and then died with CUDA out of memory. Tried to allocate 50.00 MiB. GPU 0 has a total capacity of 47.37 GiB of which 14.94 MiB is free - from TimesFM-2.5, which was never supposed to touch GPU 0. In the vendor package (timesfm/timesfm_2p5/timesfm_2p5_torch.py:72) TimesFMModel.__init__ sets self.device = torch.device("cuda:0") whenever torch.cuda.is_available() and calls self.to(self.device) inside the constructor; from_pretrained accepts no device argument, and compile() later sizes work as per_core_batch_size * model.device_count.

Two rounds of pinning failed before one worked. .to("cpu") after compile() was too late and left the cached device/device_count pointing at the GPU; pinning right after from_pretrained still OOMed because the load itself allocates there. What works (TimesFM25._load_off_gpu): when cpu was requested, hide the device for the duration of construction (torch.cuda.is_available -> False, device_count -> 0), then move the module, correct the cached attributes, and verify placement - raising UnavailableError rather than writing a row that names a device it did not run on. Verified on the saturated trux card: one series, one window, ok in 4.6 s, CPU.

The rule for every adapter: the device column is a claim you have to earn. Check next(model.parameters()).device after loading and refuse on mismatch. An adapter that ignores device= does not just run in the wrong place - it falsifies the provenance of the row, which is the one thing a benchmark row is supposed to be able to do.

docs.title: One model family is device-sensitive; the rest agree bit-for-bit across machines
docs.text:
With the data path finally held constant (both lanes reading arena directories), the GB10 replication lane and a trux lane give 216 shared cells (12 series x 2 horizons x 9 models, once the TimesFM CPU lane was re-run), gpu7 on CUDA vs trux on CPU:

model_key n cells median rel. diff (mase) max naive, seasonal_naive, arima, chronos-2, chronos-bolt-small, chronos-bolt-base, timesfm-2.5-200m, ttm-r2 24 each 0.000% 0.000% chronos-t5-small 24 3.48% 13.44%

Eight of nine families are identical to the last decimal across an aarch64/CUDA box and an x86/CPU box - which is a stronger reproducibility statement than anything this project had before. The exception is instructive: Chronos-T5 is the one path that generates (beam/ sample decoding), and generation is where a different BLAS, a different kernel, or a bf16 accumulation compounds into different sampled quantiles. Its pass-3 rows already mix CUDA (33 cells) and CPU (33 cells, the OOM retries), so those cells are not the same measurement - read device before comparing TTM-style, and treat T5 cross-device gaps of a few percent as expected rather than as a bug.

Three machines, same protocol, same bytes (2026-11-27). Watson's 35-series lane was re-run reading arena directories (reports/pass4_watson_arena: RTX A6000, CUDA, 16 models, 0 failures), so its 12 overlap series now share a data path with gpu7 and trux. Pairwise MASE on those cells:

machine pair hardware identical out of tolerance gpu7 | sedan-gpu1 GB10 CUDA | A6000 CUDA 8 of 9 families at 0.000% 18 cells, all chronos-t5-small (median 5.38%, max 11.32%) gpu7 | trux-tsubame GB10 CUDA | x86 CPU 8 of 9 families at 0.000% T5 only sedan-gpu1 | trux-tsubame A6000 CUDA | x86 CPU 8 of 9 families at 0.000% T5 only

Two CUDA stacks that share nothing - different GPU architecture, different torch build - reproduce each other exactly. That is the strongest form of the claim available, and it locates the exception in the decoding path: chronos-t5-base ran only on watson in this pass, so it still has no cross-machine pair.

The 66-series replication (pass 5, 2026-11-27) settles it. Watson re-scored gpu7's 66 series on an A6000 (reports/pass5_watson_66, node sedan-gpu3), giving 1,452 shared cells — 66 series x 2 horizons x 11 models — with gpu7 (GB10, CUDA, torch 2.9.1+cu130) and watson (A6000, CUDA, torch 2.7.1+cu128) reading the same arena bytes:

model_key cells median diff max diff cells > 2% naive, seasonal_naive, arima, theta, moving_average, chronos-2, chronos-bolt-small, chronos-bolt-base, timesfm-2.5-200m, ttm-r2 132 each 0.000% 0.000% 0 chronos-t5-small 132 5.730% 17.406% 109

Ten of eleven families are bit-identical to the last decimal on 132 cells each; every out-of-tolerance cell in the whole 1,452-cell stratum belongs to chronos-t5-small (rmse behaves the same way: median 0.000% everywhere except T5, where it reaches 23.2%). The same generator produced ttm-r2 bit-exactly, and TTM had been suspected of device sensitivity earlier — it was the context-length contract, not the device. So the rule to carry forward is narrow and checkable: anything that samples tokens at decode time may differ across stacks by several percent; everything else should be compared to zero.

The five families gpu7 had never scored (2026-11-27, reports/pass5_gpu7_extra) widen the stratum to 1,980 cells and break the tidy version of that rule. The model list made the 1,452-cell claim look wider than it was: chronos-t5-base, flowstate-r1, timesfm-3.0, ttm-r3 and patchtst-fm-r2 had been run on watson only, so they had no cross-machine pair anywhere. Scoring them on gpu7 gives 132 cells each:

model_key cells median diff max diff cells > 2% flowstate-r1 132 0.000% 0.000% 0 timesfm-3.0 132 0.000% 0.000% 0 patchtst-fm-r2 132 0.078% 0.633% 0 ttm-r3 74 0.913% 9.229% 24 chronos-t5-base 132 5.414% 29.323% 110

Three separate behaviours, and only one of them is token sampling:

  • Bit-exact (flowstate-r1, timesfm-3.0): same bytes, same protocol, identical to the last decimal on a different architecture and torch build.
  • Small drift, always inside tolerance (patchtst-fm-r2: 0.078% median, 0.63% worst cell). Not zero, so a strict "compare to zero" gate would call it a failure; it is float-order noise in an attention stack that never amplifies past a percent. Worth knowing before anyone wires a CI check that requires 0.000%.
  • Pre-existing instability, made device-visible (ttm-r3). This is the family that emitted NaN forecasts on both machines in pass 3, so its NaN policy drops a variable number of windows per stack: only 74 of its 132 cells have a MASE on both sides, and those 74 differ at 0.91% median and 9.2% worst. That is not the hardware inventing numbers; a run that is already on a cliff edge falls off it at different windows depending on rounding order. The honest reading is that ttm-r3's per-cell MASE is not a stable quantity on this corpus, on any machine.
  • Generative decoding (chronos-t5-base): 5.4% median, 29.3% worst, 110 of 132 cells outside tolerance - same signature as chronos-t5-small, larger magnitude.

So the rule survives, but the exception is bigger than "sampling at decode time": a family whose forecasts are numerically unstable on the corpus (TTM-r3) is effectively device-sensitive too, because which windows survive the NaN policy is itself a rounding-order question. Compare to zero for the bit-exact majority; expect sub-percent drift for well-conditioned attention stacks; expect several percent - and occasionally a changed denominator - for anything that samples tokens or already produces NaNs.

docs.title: A 2 MB documentation page is published but not served
docs.text:
scripts/build_docs.sh builds strictly and CI commits the site to gh-pages. The benchmark page used to be the full per-cell table (3,628 rows -> 2.19 MB of HTML). GitHub Pages returned 404 for /effectiveness/ while /matrix/ and every other page served, and the file itself was reachable at /effectiveness/index.html - a URL nothing links to, because mkdocs uses directory URLs. The page was invisible exactly where the navigation pointed.

--summary-only now generates aggregates for the site (headline ranking, provenance, interpreter table); the full per-cell table stays in the repo's merged report, which is also the readable choice.

Separately, actions/deploy-pages never worked on this account: every attempt failed with "Failed to create deployment (status: 404) ... Cannot find any run with github.run_id", both before and after the repository went public and after recreating Pages with build_type=workflow. The branch-push route (git push HEAD:gh-pages) does publish - the same mechanism the TSFM4Finance leaderboard site uses - so the docs workflow does that now.

docs.title: Re-dispatching a bridge job under a used number never runs
docs.text:
The Spark/GPU7 worker picks the first inbox/*.sh that has no matching outbox/<name>.log, because trux leaves the job file in the inbox until it is reaped and rsync would otherwise hand the same job back forever. That rule makes job numbers single-use: after job_013 ran and reported, dropping a corrected job_013 back into the inbox left it sitting there for an hour, with a live worker and a fresh heartbeat, and no error anywhere — from the worker's point of view it was already finished.

Two facts to keep separate: the run I was waiting for had actually completed (job_013.log on trux: 11 models ok / 0 failed over 66 series), and the file I re-dispatched was a stale duplicate of my own making. Housekeeping rule: a dispatch is a new number or nothing; if a name has a log, the answer is already in that log.

docs.title: The job that ran is not the job you wrote: five failures, one bridge
docs.text:
A lane for five model families on the Spark worker took six dispatches and six diagnoses to start. Nothing in it was exotic; each layer hid the previous one.

1. An unquoted value in the endpoint file silently truncated a command. bridge.env carried TRUX_SSH=ssh -i /raid/yewei/.ssh/id_ed25519_gm_transfer -o StrictHostKeyChecking=accept-new. Sourcing that line assigns TRUX_SSH="ssh" and then tries to run -i /raid/... as a command:

bridge.env: line 12: -o: command not found

The variable was non-empty, so every "is it set" check passed. The key had quietly disappeared.

2. The generator died, and its previous output was still in /tmp. gpu7_generate.sh runs under set -e, so the sourcing error above killed it before it wrote anything. The next command in the same shell was trux_dispatch.sh /tmp/job_extra5.sh - and that file existed, from the previous attempt, generated from the previous template. Dispatch queued it. The job that ran printed a corpus line the current template no longer contains, which is the only reason the mismatch was detectable at all.

3. A key path from the control plane sat in the worker's ssh config. The rsync then fell back to default ssh, and gpu7's ~/.ssh/config names IdentityFile /raid/yewei/.ssh/... - a path that exists only on trux:

Warning: Identity file /raid/yewei/.ssh/id_ed25519_gm_transfer not accessible: No such file or directory.
Permission denied, please try again.

Same symptom in job_015 and job_021, different cause each time (wrong variable in one, truncated variable in the other).

4. The corpus pull was unconditional. All 66 arena directories were already on gpu7 (missing=0 of 66 in a diagnostic job), yet the template rsynced every one of them before scoring. A two-hour lane died in its first second over bytes that did not need moving.

5. Two diagnostics were wrong before one was right. pgrep -fa inbox reported "two pollers" on gpu7; the second match was an rsync child whose command line contains the word inbox. A job that grepped for TRUX_KEY= in the templates found nothing, because the template uses $TRUX_SSH, not a key variable. The diagnostic that finally settled it printed the generated file's own header and the corpus line the job had emitted - i.e. it compared the artifact to its source instead of describing the symptom.

What the bridge does now, in order: the generator fills every placeholder (series list, control-plane endpoints, and GPU_SSH, the credential the worker holds) and refuses to emit a file containing any remaining @@TOKEN@@; it stamps the output with a generation timestamp; trux_dispatch.sh refuses a file with no stamp or a stamp older than 30 minutes; and the job itself refuses to score on a machine whose hostname is not the Spark box, because every row it writes will claim that machine as its origin. Existing corpus directories are skipped instead of re-pulled.

The general shape: a pipeline with more than one stage must refuse to consume the previous stage's leftovers. A filename in /tmp is not a proof of provenance.

docs.title: A hand-written file on a remote clone blocks the pull that brings the next job
docs.text:
Both remote harness clones stopped fast-forwarding for the same reason, an hour apart. On trux: reports/pass4_watson_arena/lane_arena.jsonl, left there as scratch output in an earlier session and committed from the laptop afterwards. On watson: probes/watson/watson_pass5_66.sh, written by hand on the remote box and committed from the laptop afterwards. Git refuses to overwrite an untracked file during a merge, so git pull --ff-only aborts with "The following untracked working tree files would be overwritten" - and a dispatch script that pipes its own output through tail -4 shows the pull line but not the abort, so the job runs on the old code and records an old code_sha.

The fix is mechanical (move the file aside, pull, compare, delete if identical), and in both cases the scratch copy was byte-identical to the committed one. The lesson is about direction of travel: artifacts written on a compute box have to come back to the control machine and into git, or they turn the compute box into an island whose pull is permanently broken. Anything worth keeping on a remote lane belongs in the repo; anything not worth keeping belongs in a directory git does not track (/scratch/<job>/).

docs.title: --max-windows draws the test windows at random, so a different seed is a different measurement
docs.text:
Reproducibility work had ruled out hardware, code drift and data path. What it had not measured was the sampling design. windows() strides the test span and, when max_windows caps the count, picks the subset uniformly at random (same seed, same windows — which is exactly why the fleet never noticed: every model on every machine used seed 0 and therefore the same windows, so cross-machine comparisons stayed bit-exact).

What seed 0 vs seed 1 means on four arena series (x86 CPU, identical bytes, identical code):

windows/cell naive's own MASE, seed-to-seed chronos-bolt MASE paired ratio model/naive 8 (fleet default) median 55%, max 100% median 54%, max 124% median 12%, max 25% 32 median 21%, max 57% median 13%, max 69% median 7%, max 17%

Read the first column again: the naive baseline's own MASE doubles between seeds. A per-cell MASE at 8 windows is a one-digit estimate, not a measurement.

What survives: paired comparisons inside one seed (every model sees the same windows), and aggregate shares over hundreds of cells — the leaderboard's "41% vs 40%" is a count across ~1,400 cells, so its noise is far smaller than any single cell's. What does not survive: calling one cell a win or a loss when its ratio sits within ~12% of parity, and any per-cell number quoted without its window count.

Two fixes, both about not letting the merge machinery blur the sample:

  • proto() — the merge's protocol signature — now carries n_windows and the lane seed, so a 32-window row cannot silently supersede an 8-window row; it becomes a supersession whose gap measures the protocol change.
  • cross_machine_check.py refuses to compare rows whose n_windows differ, as it already refuses rows whose data_hash differ.

The ranking table prints win per model and states the paired-ratio noise next to itself. For any pass whose per-cell numbers will be quoted individually, raise --max-windows to 32+ and budget roughly double the wall time.

docs.title: A partitioned corpus makes a merged report look cross-checked when it is not
docs.text:
The multi-machine fleet was designed to avoid duplicate work: watson scored 35 series, trux/gpu7 scored 66, and the two sets do not intersect. A merged 101-series report is therefore not 101 series measured twice; it is 101 series measured once each. When the pass-4 arena lanes were fed to the cross-machine checker it reported cells seen: 2546, on >=2 machines: 216 and zero gpu7-vs-watson pairs — with no disagreement flag, because there was nothing to compare.

This is the mirror image of the duplicate-key trap. Too many rows for one cell hides which measurement applies; too few rows per cell silently removes the ability to check at all. probes/watson/watson_pass5_66.sh re-scores gpu7's 66 series on the A6000 (different GPU architecture, different torch build, same arena parquet bytes) so the bit-exactness claim that currently rests on 12 series rests on 66.

Resolved the same day (pass 5). Watson re-scored gpu7's 66 series (reports/pass5_watson_66, SLURM 3291, 16 models, 0 failures). The cross-machine stratum went from 216 cells to 1,452, and the merged arena report now contains real replication for 66 of 101 series rather than a partition dressed up as coverage. The lesson generalises: a fleet that avoids duplicate work is efficient and unfalsifiable at the same time — decide before dispatching which cells will be measured twice.

docs.title: "Superseded by a fix" and "re-measured on another machine" are not the same sentence
docs.text:
The merge report classifies repeated (model, series, span, horizon) keys by their protocol signature, and until now every differing pair was described as superseded by a fix, with the gap called "the size of that fix". That was true of pass 3 (ctx 256 vs 512, CSV vs arena) and false of pass 4/5, where 1,668 pairs differ only in device, torch build and code_sha: same context, same data_hash, same window count. Calling those a correction tells a reader the older numbers were wrong; they are the reproducibility measurement, and their gap (median 0.000%, max 17.4%, all of it chronos-t5-small) is the answer to "how much does the hardware cost".

proto() is now proto_core() (what was measured: ctx, ctx_note, data_kind, data_hash, n_windows) plus the stack fields, and the report prints three buckets that mean different things: re-measured on another stack (gap = reproducibility), superseded by a protocol change (gap = the size of that change), identical signature (gap = run variance). Two tests pin the direction: the same bytes on two machines must not say "protocol change", and 8-vs-32 windows on one machine must not say "another stack".

docs.title: The GPU floor was written as a verdict, and it would have put a 200M sweep on CPU
docs.text:
gpu7_050_extra5.sh picks its device once, at launch: if torch reports less than 4 GiB free, the lane runs on CPU and says so. That was the right fix for nvidia-smi answering [N/A] on a GB10, but pass 7 exposed the other half of the problem. The audit before job_023 showed 1.1 GiB free, and this lane is 8 models x 66 series x 2 horizons at 32 and then 64 windows: ~2,100 cells of Chronos inference. On 20 CPU cores that is most of a day, on the GPU it is under an hour, and the free memory on that box swings from 1 GiB to 40 GiB within minutes because it is shared.

So the floor became a wait: pick_device polls torch every GPU_RETRY_SECS (default 120 s) for up to GPU_WAIT_SECS (default 45 min), and only then falls back to CPU - with a WARN in the log, because the device column of every row in that lane file depends on which branch was taken. The choice is also re-made per lane file, not once per job: a lane is one device for all its cells, so a decision made before a 10-hour lane would mislabel the second half of it.

Two traps this surfaced, both now tested:

  • DEV=$(pick_device) captures stdout, so the waiting for the GPU: 1173 MiB free progress line became the device string, and the sweep would have run with --device ' waiting for the GPU: 1173 MiB free ...'. A function whose return value is captured may narrate only on stderr - test_the_device_chooser_returns_only_a_device_name runs the real chooser against a stub interpreter and asserts the stdout is exactly cuda or cpu.
  • A queued bridge job is still yours until the worker claims it. The Spark worker only learns a job exists by moving it from inbox/ to inbox_done/, so until that move, mv it back and it never ran. trux_dispatch.sh --hold makes that deliberate: stage a generated job in hold/ (no number allocated, stamp still validated), release it later with the same command. job_023 was withdrawn this way after the memory audit; job_024 is the version above.

And while wiring the --hold test: trux_dispatch.sh --hold job.sh read --hold as the job path and rejected it for missing a GENERATED stamp, and the repo's own bridge.env.example still carried the unquoted-ssh-value bug that killed job_021 (TRUX_SSH=ssh -i ... assigns ssh, then the shell tries to run -i). Both are pinned: flags are now parsed positionally with an explicit unknown-flag failure, and every multi-word value in the example is quoted and sourced by a test.

docs.title: The beat-naive share is a threshold on a noisy number, and 32 windows lowers every model's share
docs.text:
Pass 7 re-scored the same 66 arena series on the same watson node at 32 windows instead of 8 (reports/pass7_watson_win, 8 models, same bytes, same seed, n_windows in the protocol signature so nothing merges across the two). The headline result is not a tie resolving - it is that every model's beat-naive share falls, and the ordering moves with it:

The 64-window pass (same node, same bytes) is included to show where it stops moving: 32 is already the plateau, so the extra cost of 64 buys nothing.

model beat naive @ 8w @ 32w @ 64w 8w → 32w 32w → 64w arima 56.1% 40.9% 44.7% -15.2 pp +3.8 pp chronos-bolt-small 42.4% 15.2% 15.9% -27.3 pp +0.7 pp chronos-2 39.4% 22.0% 13.6% -17.4 pp -8.4 pp theta 34.1% 15.9% 13.6% -18.2 pp -2.3 pp chronos-bolt-base 32.6% 12.1% 11.4% -20.5 pp -0.7 pp chronos-t5-small 33.3% 9.1% 9.8% -24.2 pp +0.7 pp seasonal_naive 17.4% 6.8% 4.5% -10.6 pp -2.3 pp

Head-to-head on the same cells (8w / 32w / 64w):

pair 8w 32w 64w reading arima > chronos-bolt-small 58.3% 84.1% 83.3% real, and far bigger than 8 windows showed chronos-2 > chronos-t5-small 55.3% 69.7% 70.5% real chronos-bolt-small > chronos-2 53.8% 40.2% 38.6% the 8-window "tie" resolves against bolt-small chronos-bolt-base > chronos-t5-small 48.5% 50.0% 47.0% genuinely a tie: it does not move

The published table is internally inconsistent at 8 windows, not just noisy. A tie that becomes a 61%-to-39% gap when the window sample quadruples was never a tie; it was the sample. 33.0% of cells (305/924) change winner between 8 and 64 windows.

Why: the share counts a cell as a win when mase_model < mase_naive, i.e. when a noisy ratio lands below 1.0. The ratio distributions show both halves of the problem at once - the 8-window draws are wider and sit closer to parity:

model median ratio @8w IQR @8w within ±10% of parity @8w median @32w IQR @32w within ±10% @32w chronos-bolt-small 1.029 [0.956, 1.134] 60.6% 1.053 [1.012, 1.086] 81.1% chronos-2 1.023 [0.975, 1.076] 78.8% 1.032 [1.004, 1.066] 84.1% chronos-bolt-base 1.037 [0.978, 1.136] 62.1% 1.076 [1.026, 1.126] 62.1% arima 1.000 [0.997, 1.002] 100% 1.001 [0.998, 1.003] 100%

Centre the noise on a value that is already just above 1, and a threshold at 1.0 counts far more false wins than true ones: at 8 windows 60.6% of chronos-bolt-small's cells are inside ±10% of parity, and 32.3% of all cells (256/792) change winner between 8 and 32 windows. A single cell at this resolution was never a measurement of model quality; it was a measurement of that window draw. arima is the extreme case and also the reason it tops the table: its fitted forecasts are indistinguishable from persistence on these series (median ratio 1.000, IQR 0.005), so it neither wins nor loses - it is naive with extra steps, and its "share" is pure coin-toss mass around parity.

Cross-machine at the new protocol (reports/pass7_watson_win/lane_win32.jsonl vs reports/pass7_trux_win/lane_cuda-?.jsonl, 990 shared cells: watson A6000 CUDA vs trux RTX 6000 Ada CUDA and trux CPU, same bytes, seed 0): seven of eight families 0.000% median and 0.000% max (132 cells each), chronos-t5-small again the only outlier - and its median falls from 5.73% (8 windows, pass 5) to 2.165% (32 windows). The generative family's stack sensitivity was partly window noise all along. chronos-t5-small OOM'd on trux's GPU mid-lane (another user's process held 26.6 GiB of 47.4); the lane file records it as a failed model with the CUDA error, and the CPU lane covered those 33 series - which is why the surviving t5 pair is CUDA-vs-CPU, and why the device column is part of the number and not decoration.

What this changes: * The default window count for any pass whose numbers get quoted is 32, not 8 (sweep_evaluate.py defaults to 32 as of pass 7). 8 windows is fine for a smoke test of whether a family runs at all (which is what it was used for). Pass 7b (probes/watson/watson_pass7b_rest32.sh) moves the other 11 model keys to 32 windows on the same 66 series so the published table shares one protocol. * Shares from an 8-window pass must be published with the window count next to them. The generator now prints win per model in the ranking table, and proto() keys on n_windows, so an 8-window row can never supersede a 32-window one. * probes/window_sensitivity.py reproduces every number above (probes/window_sensitivity.py reports/pass5_watson_66/lane.jsonl reports/pass7_watson_win/lane_win32.jsonl), and tests/test_window_sensitivity.py pins that the probe keeps window counts as separate groups and counts flips per cell.

docs.title: A row's n_windows is what survived scoring, not what was asked for
docs.text:
The first version of probes/window_sensitivity.py grouped cells by the row's n_windows, which is the obvious field and the wrong one. Three results came out of one 64-window lane: groups at 38, 39, 40, 49, 50 and 64 windows. Nothing was broken in the sweep - n_windows is the number of windows that survived scoring (evaluate.py sets it to len(kept) after NaN/blank windows leave the set), and a series whose test span holds 39 candidate windows cannot score 64 no matter what was requested. So one protocol fragmented into six groups, and a short series scored under a 32-window budget looks identical to the same series under an 8-window budget.

That second half is the dangerous part, and it reaches the merge, not just the probe: if the protocol signature only sees the scored count, a 32-window row silently supersedes an 8-window row for a capped series, and the corpus changes under the table while every duplicate-classification label stays "re-measured on another stack".

Both are fixed at the source: * proto_core() now carries the requested budget (max_windows, from the lane meta and stamped on every row by stamp_rows) alongside the scored count. The pinned case: two rows identical in every scored field, requested 8 vs 32 → different proto_core, so different protocol (tests/test_merge_sections.py::test_a_wider_window_request_is_a_different_protocol_even_when_the_series_caps_it). * The probe groups by the requested budget (row field, else lane meta, else scored count with a printed note), and a test feeds a lane where one cell scored 39 under a 64-window request and asserts no 39 windows: group appears (tests/test_window_sensitivity.py).

The general rule: a field that records what happened during scoring cannot stand in for what was requested. The request is the protocol; the score count is a property of the cell.

docs.title: An untracked config file beside the script outranked the operator's own variable
docs.text:
Five bridge tests passed on the laptop and failed on trux with no code change between them. trux_dispatch.sh sources probes/trux/bridge/bridge.env (untracked: hostnames, keys, the queue path) after the caller's environment is set, so on trux that file's BRIDGE= overwrote the fixture path a test exported - the test was reading the live inbox. Same script, two machines, two behaviours, and the failure looked like a bug in the numbering logic rather than in test isolation.

bridge.env is now defaults only: an exported BRIDGE survives sourcing it, in both trux_dispatch.sh and gpu7_generate.sh, pinned by tests/test_bridge_generate.py::test_an_explicit_BRIDGE_beats_the_bridge_env_next_to_the_script. The same lesson as the hand-written file that pinned a remote clone to old code: config that lives outside git changes behaviour per machine, so it must be a default with an explicit override, never the last word.

docs.title: 09 · Running this as a benchmark
docs.text: The compatibility matrix answers "does this architecture work here at all". A benchmark answers a different question: "how well does it forecast, and how do the architectures compare". Both run through the same API, and conflating them is the most common way to over-claim from this repo, so the two are kept formally separate here.

docs.title: The two claims, in one table
docs.text:
question command what a ✅ / a number means compatibility can the architecture be loaded, forecast, be scored, and be reached by a training/RL path in this environment tsfm-trl doctor → COMPATIBILITY.md the code ran end-to-end at smoke size; nothing about accuracy effectiveness how accurate is it, and how does it compare across families, horizons, domains tsfm-trl evaluate (forecast_eval) numbers on held-out windows with a defined metric, split and seed

COMPATIBILITY.md deliberately contains no accuracy numbers. Its fine-tune column carries a two-step loss for one reason only: to prove the objective is differentiable and the logging works. Reading it as "fine-tuning helped" is a category error (docs/03_fine_tune.md).

docs.title: Metrics that exist (all hand-written, all NaN-safe)
docs.text:
tsfm_trl/eval/metrics.py, on the canonical LEVELS grid unless stated otherwise:

family function note point rmse, mae, mape, smape, nd scale-free ones (nd, smape) for cross-series comparison scale-free skill mase, relative_skill both need the training span and a season (1 for the finance panels) direction directional_accuracy anchor-relative: the last observed value by default, which is the version that matters for the finance labels (docs/07_finance_tasks.md) ranking rank_corr per-window Spearman, useful for signal-style tasks probabilistic pinball, crps_from_quantiles, wql, quantile_coverage quantile-based; coverage only counts bands the model actually emits — a model that ships 9 levels is not scored on 21 classification classification_report PR-AUC (multiclass OVR), ROC-AUC, macro-F1, F2-beta, precision/recall, base rate; hard labels give nan for PR/ROC rather than a fabricated score

forecast_report(y, pred, train) bundles the point + probabilistic set into one dict; forecast_eval(...) produces one row per (span, horizon).

docs.title: Protocol
docs.text:
The library fixes the parts of a protocol that would otherwise differ per family:

  • one quantile grid (LEVELS, 21 levels) — adapters that emit fewer levels are mapped onto their own subset and Pred.meta["levels_emitted"] records it;
  • one normalisation of the question — anchor-relative targets for the finance labels, and the model's own scaler is never re-implemented outside the adapter;
  • context handling — ctx_step/max_context per adapter, left-padding with the model's own pad mask instead of zeros (Moirai, FlowState) — a silent zero-pad changes the score for patch models; and min_context for checkpoints that declare a fixed input length (Granite/TTM): the evaluation window is raised to it, or padded with the oldest observation when the span cannot supply it, because feeding a shorter window makes those models pad themselves and scale the answer by the padded fraction;
  • split discipline — SeriesDataset.splits, and any checkpoint carries split_end so load_finetuned can refuse an evaluation window that overlaps training.

Budget names in TrainingConfig are also evaluation sizes:

BUDGETS = {"fs16": 16 windows / 40 steps / lr 1e-5,
           "fs64": 64 windows / 120 steps / lr 1e-5,
           "full": all windows / 3 epochs / lr 5e-6}

docs.title: Running an effectiveness pass
docs.text:
One model, several horizons, JSON rows out (stdout is a data channel — progress lines go to stderr):

tsfm-trl evaluate --model chronos-2 --series px.csv --horizons 21,63,126 --ctx 512
tsfm-trl evaluate --model chronos-2 --adaptation reports/ft/chronos-2__…/model.pt \
                  --series px.csv --horizons 21,63

The second form is the zero-shot-vs-adapted comparison: the checkpoint's provenance (base id, peft level, trained parameter names, split_end) is validated on load, so the comparison cannot silently swap a TimesFM head onto a Moirai trunk or evaluate on windows the run trained on.

The whole registry at once, one interpreter per family, one row per model per series per horizon — this is what produced EFFECTIVENESS.md (rendered as the site's Measured effectiveness page):

# canonical series: fev-style directories with real train/validation/test splits and
# OHLCV covariates (panel-consuming models such as Kronos need them)
scripts/sweep_evaluate.py \
    --series data/open/sp500_long --series data/open/audusd --series data/open/btc_crypto \
    --horizons 21,63,126 --max-windows 12 --spans all \
    --out reports/effectiveness_dgx.jsonl --fresh

# merge several machines/runs; merging is per (model, series, span, horizon), so partial
coverage from different machines unions instead of overwriting, and every row keeps the
machine/interpreter/torch stamp of the run that produced it
scripts/sweep_evaluate.py --report reports/effectiveness_dgx.jsonl,\
reports/effectiveness_watson.jsonl,reports/effectiveness_laptop_vendor.jsonl \
    --md EFFECTIVENESS.md

The sweep refuses to run a model in an environment the registry does not name for it (a missing env is a recorded skip, not a core fallback), writes rows to JSONL as they land, and stamps each run with its machine, series, spans and window count — so a published table can always be traced to the interpreter that produced each row.

Reward runs get the same treatment: scripts/reward_seeds.py --model … --seeds 0,1,2 reports the spread of the late-minus-early reward delta instead of one curve.

Through the API, which is what a sweep should use:

from tsfm_trl import ModelHub
from tsfm_trl.eval.evaluate import forecast_eval

m = ModelHub.load("moirai-1.1-R-small", device="cuda", ctx_cap=512, batch=16)
rows = forecast_eval(m, "panels/px.csv", horizons=(21, 63, 126),
                     spans=("test",), ctx=512, max_windows=64, seed=0, season=1)

Across environments, use the same subprocess dispatch the matrix uses — one interpreter per family (envs/local.json), because the family pins are mutually contradictory (docs/01_install.md):

tsfm-trl doctor --all-envs --tasks load,predict,quantiles \
                --json reports/matrix_bench_core.json

predict is the benchmark's inference half: every row that is ✅ there can be dropped into forecast_eval without further adaptation work.

docs.title: Sampling noise (measured 2026-11-27, four arena series, same bytes, same code)
docs.text:
--max-windows draws the test windows uniformly at random; same seed, same windows. At the fleet default of 8 windows per cell, seed 0 vs seed 1 moves naive's own MASE by ~55% median (max 100%), a model's MASE by ~54%, and the paired model/naive ratio by ~12% (max 25%). At 32 windows: ~21%, ~13%, ~7%. So aggregate shares over hundreds of cells are trustworthy, a single cell within ~12% of parity is not a win or a loss, and n_windows + lane seed are part of the merge protocol signature (proto) and a hard precondition in cross_machine_check.py.

The noise does not average out symmetrically, because the headline statistic is a threshold. Pass 7 re-scored the same 66 series on the same node at 32 windows: every model's beat-naive share fell (chronos-bolt-small 42.4% -> 15.2%, arima 56.1% -> 40.9%), the head-to-head chronos-bolt-small > chronos-2 moved 53.8% -> 40.2%, and 32.3% of cells change winner between the two window counts. Cause: the per-cell model/naive ratio is centred just above 1 with a wide spread at 8 windows, so counting cells below 1.0 collects more false wins than true ones. Table and mechanism in docs/08 ("The beat-naive share is a threshold on a noisy number"); reproduce with probes/window_sensitivity.py. The 64-window pass says where it stops: 32w vs 64w shares differ by at most 8 pp, so 32 is enough. Consequence for this document: every share in the tables below is an 8-window number and is labelled as such; any pass whose numbers will be quoted runs at --max-windows 32 (now the default of sweep_evaluate.py).

docs.title: Reporting rules (what goes in a table, what does not)
docs.text:
1. Report the metric family the model can serve. A point-only head (TTM r2/r3) has no CRPS; write —, do not integrate a degenerate distribution. Same reason TiRex's NPP and Chronos-Bolt's samples both get empirical quantiles first: different routes to the same grid, then the same metric.
  2. Report coverage per emitted band and say which bands (Pred.meta).
  3. One row per (model, environment); a model that is ✅ on one machine and OOM on another is a fact about the machine, and the matrix keeps both under other machine.
  4. State the parameter budget for adapted rows — peft="lora" now means a frozen trunk, and TrainResult.trainable_parameters is the number to print (docs/08_known_issues.md explains why that sentence exists).
  5. Multiple seeds and windows. A single 16-window pass is a smoke test; the harness defaults are deliberately smoke-sized (fs16/fs64) so an accidental 10-hour run is impossible by default.
  6. Baselines in the same table. naive, seasonal_naive, theta, arima, moving_average are registered models with their own rows, so every effectiveness table can carry skill relative to them (relative_skill, MASE) rather than raw loss.

docs.title: What pass 1 shows (and what it does not license)
docs.text:
43 of 46 registry models have rows; the three that do not are named in the table with their reason (TimeMoE ran out of a 6 GB laptop GPU, TiRex-2's mLSTM kernels fail on this toolchain, VisionTS++ ships weights with no installable package). All numbers are zero-shot, one seed, 12 windows per pass, on three daily series.

  • No published checkpoint beats the trivial scaler on point accuracy at these horizons. On sp500_long every model — statistical baseline or foundation model — has MASE above ~4 at h=21 and above ~9 at h=126. MASE normalises by the in-sample mean |Δ| of the training span, so this says: at three-week and half-year horizons on a daily index, the level scale dominates and none of these weights produce point-forecast skill over "tomorrow ≈ today".
  • Directional accuracy sits at 0.5. The best cells in the dir-acc column are ~0.53–0.59 and many are below 0.5, which is what noise looks like. For a finance benchmark that is the headline result, not a caveat.
  • What does separate the models is calibration. On sp500_long at h=21 TiRex's nominal 80% band covers 0.81 (close to nominal), Chronos-T5-base's covers 0.74, and ARIMA's covers 0.98 — ARIMA's intervals are simply too wide. At h=126 on btc_crypto, coverage collapses for the same models (TiRex 0.27, ARIMA 0.30): long crypto bands from these weights are not usable as stated. A point-only model cannot even be charged with this failure, which is why the pt marker matters.
  • Ranking is not stable across series or horizon. TiRex and Moirai-1.1-R-base lead on the index; Moirai-2.0-R-small and t0-gamma lead on crypto at h=126. Anyone quoting "X is the best TSFM" from one dataset is quoting noise.
  • The benchmark found a library bug the compatibility matrix could not. TiRex's roll-forward path for horizons longer than one vendor output block mixed the batch axis into a 1-D context and raised — at h ≤ 63 (the matrix grid) that code never ran, so the model "worked". It is now fixed and measurable, and it happens to be the best zero-shot point model on the index. A green ✅ in a capability matrix is evidence the call returned, not that the numbers are right.

What this does not license: any statement about a family being better in general (12 windows, one seed, three daily series), anything about adapted checkpoints (not run), or the word "significant" (no variance estimate exists for a forecast row).

docs.title: What pass 3 shows (the whole standard/ corpus: 101 series, 3,628 cells)
docs.text:
Scope: every one of the 101 independent per-instrument series in standard/, 19 models, horizons 21 and 63, 8 windows per series, one seed, zero-shot. Series were split 66/35 between trux (2× RTX 6000 Ada, core+moment+timemoe envs) and watson (one A6000 via SLURM, core only), disjoint, allocated 2:1 inside every dataset family so neither machine's table is confounded with one family. Merged per (model, series, span, horizon).

Median MASE relative to the naive scaler on the same cell (1.00 = equal), share of cells where the model beat naive:

model cells beat naive med MASE/naive med MASE cov@40 ctx arima 202 55% 1.00 4.50 0.47 256 chronos-2 202 40% 1.02 4.66 0.38 256 chronos-bolt-small 202 41% 1.03 4.73 0.38 256 theta 202 30% 1.04 4.79 — 256 chronos-bolt-base 202 32% 1.04 4.99 0.39 256 chronos-t5-base 202 35% 1.05 4.99 0.33 256 chronos-t5-small 202 35% 1.05 4.90 0.33 256 timesfm-2.5-200m 202 29% 1.06 4.89 0.36 256 timesfm-3.0 202 29% 1.07 4.95 0.35 256 seasonal_naive 202 19% 1.08 4.82 — 256 flowstate-r1 202 20% 1.10 5.01 0.21 256 patchtst-fm-r2 202 20% 1.14 5.37 — 256 moving_average 202 13% 1.21 5.42 — 256 ttm-r2 202 27% 1.25 5.70 — 512 timemoe-50m 132 6% 1.47 6.56 0.38 256 moment-1-small 132 1% 2.64 12.13 — 256 (head untrained) moment-1-large 132 1% 2.66 12.02 — 256 (head untrained) ttm-r3 168 1% 3.75 17.60 — 512
  • On 101 financial series, no foundation model beats a well-tuned ARIMA at h=21/63. ARIMA leads the corpus (55% of cells better than naive, median ratio 1.00); the strongest transformers are at parity or slightly worse (Chronos-2 40%, Chronos-Bolt-small 41%, TimesFM 29%). This is the headline of the benchmark, and it is a statement about zero-shot weights on daily/hourly price data at three-week and quarter horizons.
  • A green matrix cell and a correct number are different things, twice over. MOMENT scored because we rebuild its task head, but the checkpoint never trained one (flagged, head_from_checkpoint: false). TTM was scored at ctx 256 while its checkpoint declares 512 and pads shorter input with zeros, which scaled its whole forecast by the fraction of real history and produced a median MASE of 13x naive. Honouring the contract moved r2 from 1.51 to 1.25 and made r3's real weakness visible instead of hiding it behind the artifact.
  • ttm-r3 is unstable on this corpus, and the harness now says so in the row. 272 of 3,232 forecast windows came back non-finite (416 on CPU lanes, 272 on CUDA - so not a device artifact), and 34 of 202 cells scored nothing. Those cells report pred_nan_windows and an error, n_windows counts only what was scored, and no metric column carries a NaN.

  • Model coverage differs across the corpus and the table shows it: MOMENT and TimeMoE ran only on trux's 66 series (no moment/timemoe env on watson), chronos-t5-base has 33 CUDA cells plus 33 CPU cells after a shared-card OOM. ctx and device are per-row facts, not footnotes.

  • These numbers are reproducible - across machines and across re-runs. On unscaled metrics the machines agree bit-for-bit: RMSE matched to ~1e-8 and directional accuracy was identical when gpu7 (DGX Spark, GB10) re-scored watson's series (probes/trux/ cross_machine_check.py), and 254 repeated cell comparisons on one machine - pass-3 lanes at code sha 1d2f3ae re-scored at 28fd7e7 - agree to within 0.143%. That is the first time this benchmark has had a consistency check rather than an assumption.

  • Cross-machine, same data path: bit-exact for ten of eleven families. gpu7 (GB10, CUDA, torch 2.9.1+cu130) vs watson (RTX A6000, CUDA, torch 2.7.1+cu128) over 1,452 shared cells (66 series x 2 horizons x 11 models, same arena parquet bytes): ten families agree at 0.000% median and 0.000% max on all 132 cells each; chronos-t5-small is the only outlier (median 5.73%, max 17.4%, 109 of 132 cells). A third machine (trux, x86 CPU) reproduces the same numbers bit-exactly for the same families. The exception tracks the decoding path (T5 samples tokens; nothing else in the fleet does), not the hardware.

  • Scaled metrics are only comparable within a data path. The 12-series GB10 overlap looked like 212 machine disagreements: MASE off by 15%-123% while RMSE agreed to the eighth decimal. Cause: watson's pass-3 lane read exported CSVs (so SeriesDataset synthesized a 70/15/15 split) and the trux/gpu7 lanes read arena directories (the publisher's split), and MASE is divided by the naive error of whichever train split was loaded. For std_equity_1d_10104: 0.375671 vs 0.431936, reciprocal ratio 1.1498 - exactly the observed MASE ratio, to four decimals. Rows now carry data_hash (values + split boundaries) and data_kind, the lane meta carries data_kinds, the merge files such a repeat under supersessions, and the cross-machine check exits "inconclusive" instead of "disagreement". beats naive per cell survives this (the baseline shares the denominator); absolute MASE columns across the watson block (CSV) and the trux block (arena dirs) do not.

  • Repeated cell keys are mostly a protocol being replaced, not noise. The pass-3 merge inputs carry 404 (model, series, span, horizon) keys measured more than once. Scored by protocol signature (ctx, ctx_note, device, code_sha, torch), they are overwhelmingly supersessions - a TTM cell at ctx 256 (the zero-padding artifact, MASE 30.1) and the same cell at its contract ctx 512 (MASE 4.3). Reading that spread as run variance would blame the noise floor for the bug we removed. The merge now splits the two readings and reports each separately; only identical-signature repeats are quoted as variance.
  • A row's model field is the adapter's family key, not the registry key, and ten checkpoints collide on it (chronos-bolt-base and -small both write chronos-bolt; kronos-base/-mini/-small all write kronos-small). Grouping results by that field merges different checkpoints and manufactures disagreement — it is exactly how a "3-40% cross-machine discrepancy" appeared and disappeared in this session's notes. Rows now carry model_key; the merge always keyed on the registry key.

What this does not license: any variance claim (one seed, 8 windows per cell), any statement about fine-tuned checkpoints, or cross-context comparison of TTM against the 256-point models without reading the ctx column. Reproduce the table with probes/trux/rank_pass3.py over the merged JSONL files.

docs.title: The one fine-tune measurement in this benchmark (MOMENT, watson A6000)
docs.text:
The matrix says which families can be fine-tuned; only MOMENT has zero-shot and fine-tuned cells on the same series, because its zero-shot forecast head is randomly initialised and fine-tuning is the only way it becomes a forecaster. 12 series, ctx 256, 120 fit steps from the train span, scored on the test span (reports/moment_ft_watson/lane_ft.jsonl, read it with probes/watson/moment_ft_report.py). MASE as a ratio to naive, median over the 12:

adaptation lr h=21 h=63 zero-shot (head untrained) - 2.56 2.14 heads_only 1e-6 2.42 2.12 heads_only default 2.18 1.71 heads_only 1e-4 1.67 1.55 full fine-tune default 1.70 1.54
  • Fine-tuning the head closes about a third of the gap and no more: MOMENT goes from 2.6x naive to 1.67x naive and still loses to naive on 11 of 12 series. Some individual cells do beat it (best 0.72 of naive at h=63), which is what you would expect on the few series with structure a reconstruction-trained encoder can see.
  • Learning rate mattered more than which weights were trainable. lr 1e-6 barely moved the number (2.42, close to zero-shot); lr 1e-4 with only the head trainable matched full fine-tuning of the whole model. A fine-tune comparison that leaves lr at a framework default can conclude "this family does not adapt" when the truth is "this lr does nothing".
  • Every fine-tuned row carries head_from_checkpoint: false, head_trained_here: true, so the table cannot be misread as a pretrained forecast head.

docs.title: What passes 4-6 show: 101 series on one data path, with intervals
docs.text:
Pass 4 scored the corpus on a single arena-parquet data path (gpu7 66 series + watson the other 35, horizons 21/63). Pass 5 had watson re-score gpu7's 66 series; pass 6 added the two families that had never been cross-checked (moment-1-small, moment-1-large, timemoe-50m: watson on an A6000, trux on CPU) and scored the five families gpu7 had skipped (chronos-t5-base, flowstate-r1, timesfm-3.0, ttm-r3, patchtst-fm-r2). The merged table is now 3,628 rows over 101 series from 8 lane files on 4 machines, and 1,980 of those cells were measured twice on two stacks that share nothing (66 series x 2 horizons x 15 model keys). That is what turns the corpus from a partition into a sample with replication: the merge report classifies all 2,064 repeated pairs as "same bytes, same protocol, different stack", with no protocol changes hiding inside them.

The ranking lives in EFFECTIVENESS.md; what belongs here is the uncertainty around it (probes/pass4_share_bootstrap.py, cluster bootstrap over series, each series moving as a block because its two horizons are not independent):

model cells beat naive 95% CI arima 202 55.4% 48.0 .. 62.9 (101 series) chronos-bolt-small 202 41.1% 34.7 .. 47.5 (101 series) chronos-2 202 39.6% 33.2 .. 45.5 (101 series) chronos-bolt-base 202 32.2% 25.7 .. 39.1 (101 series) chronos-t5-small 202 31.7% 24.8 .. 38.6 (101 series) chronos-t5-base 202 30.7% 24.3 .. 37.1 (101 series) theta 202 30.2% 24.3 .. 36.6 (101 series) timesfm-2.5-200m 202 29.2% 23.3 .. 34.7 (101 series) timesfm-3.0 202 29.2% 23.8 .. 34.7 (101 series) ttm-r2 202 26.7% 20.3 .. 33.7 (101 series) seasonal_naive 202 19.3% 14.4 .. 24.3 (101 series) flowstate-r1 202 19.3% 13.4 .. 25.2 (101 series) patchtst-fm-r2 202 18.8% 13.9 .. 24.3 (101 series) moving_average 202 12.9% 8.4 .. 17.8 (101 series) timemoe-50m 132 6.1% 2.3 .. 9.8 (66 series) ttm-r3 126 0.8% 0.0 .. 2.4 (63 series) moment-1-small 132 0.8% 0.0 .. 2.3 (66 series) moment-1-large 132 0.8% 0.0 .. 2.3 (66 series)

These shares are 8-window numbers, and that is a level error, not just noise. Pass 7 re-scored the 8-model tie cluster on the same 66 series and node at 32 and 64 windows: every share falls (arima 56.1% -> 40.9% -> 44.7%, chronos-bolt-small 42.4% -> 15.2% -> 15.9%, chronos-2 39.4% -> 22.0% -> 13.6%), 33.0% of cells change winner between 8 and 64 windows, and 32 is already the plateau (32w -> 64w moves shares by <= 8 pp while 8w -> 32w moves them by 10-27 pp). Head-to-head on the same cells: arima > chronos-bolt-small 58.3% -> 83.3%, chronos-2 > chronos-t5-small 55.3% -> 70.5%, and the "tie" chronos-bolt-small vs chronos-2 resolves against bolt-small (53.8% -> 38.6%). Only chronos-bolt-base vs chronos-t5-small stays a tie at every window count (48.5/50.0/ 47.0). The intervals below measure corpus sampling, not window sampling; the two errors are independent and both are in the number. Pass 7b (probes/watson/watson_pass7b_rest32.sh plus a trux lane run) moves the other 11 model keys to 32 windows so the whole table shares one protocol; until it lands the ranks below are 8-window ranks, and probes/pass7_merge_files.txt is the merge that replaces them (it deliberately excludes the 8-window lanes - a share at 8 windows is a different measurement, not an earlier draft of the same one). See docs/08 and probes/window_sensitivity.py.

What that says, and what it does not:

  • arima over every foundation model is real. It wins the paired comparison against chronos-bolt-small in 99.9% of resamples and chronos-2 in 100.0%. Intervals barely touch.
  • chronos-bolt-small vs chronos-2 is a tie, not 41% > 40%. Pairwise 61.6% - a mildly favoured coin flip. Publishing them as ranks 2 and 3 is over-precision.
  • chronos-bolt-base vs chronos-t5-small is 53.8% at 8 windows and stays a tie at 32 and 64 (50.0%, 47.0% head-to-head): this one is a real tie, which is why it survives the protocol change.

A model whose interval overlaps a neighbour's is tied as far as this pass can see. Raising --max-windows narrows these intervals roughly as 1/sqrt(windows); scoring more series narrows the series-level part, which is the part the bootstrap measures.

docs.title: What is not done yet (so nobody reads it in)
docs.text:
• The effectiveness sweep that has been run is zero-shot only: 46 registry models × 3 canonical series (sp500_long, audusd, btc_crypto) × horizons 21/63/126, 12 windows per pass, one seed, on three machines (DGX Spark aarch64, an x86 node with an RTX A6000, and a 6 GB laptop for the vendor-family models). The result lives in EFFECTIVENESS.md (rendered as the site's Measured effectiveness page).
  • What that does not cover: more than one seed (so no confidence intervals on any cell), more datasets or frequencies (three daily series is a start, not GIFT-Eval), adapted checkpoints (--spans test + --adaptation <ckpt>, never all), and any statement that a family is "better" — with one seed and twelve windows a MASE ordering is a measurement, not a verdict.
  • No multi-seed confidence intervals, no Diebolt–Mariano / MZ statistics, no horizon-grid plots.
  • The finance label set (dir5, extreme) and a tiny public UEA/UCR subset are wired for classification; external-validity classification numbers across all 46 models are not in the repo either.
  • Fine-tune effectiveness (does adaptation improve out-of-sample skill, per family, at a stated parameter budget) is a separate experiment that the checkpoint provenance format is designed to make auditable, and has not been run at benchmark scale.

If a paper table is the goal, the honest structure is: compatibility matrix (this repo, complete), effectiveness table (to run: evaluate across families × horizons × budgets, with baselines), adaptation table (zero-shot vs LoRA at a stated budget, for the 29 families where the training path exists).

docs.title: RL / reward API
docs.text:
The post-training layer of tsfm-trl: what RewardTrainer does, what it needs from an adapter, and which architectures can actually be pushed with reward. Everything here is about capability — "this architecture accepts this kind of post-training in this environment" — not about whether the model got better on held-out data.

Read the numbers as capability

The reward column of the measured matrix answers which path exists and runs. Effectiveness is a separate measurement with its own protocol, and the honest demonstrators at the bottom of this page include negative results.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
from tsfm_trl import ModelHub
from tsfm_trl.data.fixtures import tiny_finance
from tsfm_trl.doctor import _wins                    # (context, truth) pairs, train split only
from tsfm_trl.training.config import TrainingConfig
from tsfm_trl.training.reward import RewardTrainer, RewardSpec

model = ModelHub.load("chronos-t5-small", device="cuda", ctx_cap=256, batch=8)
cfg = TrainingConfig(ctx=256, horizon=21, budget="fs64", peft="lora", device="cuda")
data = {"windows": _wins(ds.split("train"), 256, 21, 64), "info": {"series": "fx"}}

res = RewardTrainer(model, cfg, n_candidates=8, kl=0.02, spec=RewardSpec()).fit(data)
print(res.status, res.extra["mode"], res.extra["reward_early_mean"],
      res.extra["reward_late_mean"], res.extra["improved"], res.extra["fallbacks"])

tsfm-trl reward --model chronos-t5-small --steps 48 --bs 8 --lr 2e-5 \
                --budget fs64 --peft lora --device cuda
tsfm-trl reward --model toto-2-22m --mode rft            # pin the path explicitly
tsfm-trl reward --model ttm-r2 --mode grpo               # honest failure if it can't do GRPO

--mode accepts auto | rft | grpo | reward_descent | reward_descent_point | none. auto walks the ladder below and records every fallback; an explicit mode does not fall back silently, so a pinned mode is how you prove which path an architecture has.

docs.title: The reward
docs.text:
Default reward (RewardSpec), per window, over the horizon:

scale   = q_hi − q_lo            # the model's own spread; falls back to |candidate| mean
point   = −|truth − candidate| / scale              scale-free accuracy
dirn    = sign(candidate − anchor) · sign(truth − anchor)
r       = clip( −w_pinball·point + w_dir·dirn , ±clip ).mean(horizon)

with w_pinball=1.0, w_dir=0.5, w_cross=0.2 (crossing-quantile penalty on the numpy path), clip=50. anchor is the last observed value of the context, so the direction term means "did the forecast point the right way away from where the series stood" — which is what a finance benchmark cares about, and why accuracy alone is not enough: a flat forecast can be accurate and useless.

Scale-free by construction: rewards are comparable across series and across models, because the denominator is the model's own uncertainty, not a per-series constant. A custom reward= callable replaces it and must keep the (B, K) shape returned by reward_candidates.

docs.title: The four paths
docs.text:
mode what the update is requires from the adapter who has it grpo sample K paths per window, group-relative advantage A, update −A·logp on the sampled token sequence sample_paths() and path_logprob() Chronos-T5 only rft best-of-N rejection sampling: score K candidates, supervised step toward the best one sample_paths() or a sampler on the inference path 18 models (diffusion, autoregressive-token, mixture heads) reward_descent gradient ascent on the reward through the head forward_quantiles() (differentiable quantile head) 5 models reward_descent_point same, on the point head when the quantile head lacks the needed levels differentiable point head 5 models — no trainable path in the public build — 15 declined

grpo is the only path that is RL in the policy-gradient sense. rft is rejection-sampling fine-tuning (the shape most TSFM papers use); descent is not RL at all — it is differentiable-optimisation of a reward. The distinction is kept in the matrix on purpose: a table that calls all of these "RL" hides which architectures are actually policy-optimisable.

docs.title: Ladder
docs.text:
mode="auto" tries, in order of invasiveness, and records each step in extra["fallbacks"]:

grpo → reward_descent → reward_descent_point → rft

plus budget fallbacks (bs→1, amp, peft → heads_only) when the attempt runs out of memory. Every fallback that was taken is in the result and in the matrix row's reason — a mode you did not ask for is a finding, not a detail. TSFMTRL_DEBUG=1 prints the traceback of each rejected rung instead of only its message.

docs.title: Adapter contract (what makes a model RL-able)
docs.text:
method feeds used by trainable() the module to put parameters under training all modes (None → the row is declined) training_step(contexts, truth, horizon) a differentiable loss fine-tune, rft's supervised step forward_quantiles(...) differentiable quantiles reward_descent sample_paths(...) K candidate paths, no log-probs needed grpo, rft path_logprob(paths) log-probability of a given token path grpo only

path_logprob is the scarce one: it exists only for discrete-token models with explicit vocabulary logits (Chronos-T5). Diffusion/flow heads (Sundial, Kronos), mixture-of quantiles (Moirai 1.1) and continuous regression heads (TTM, MOMENT) can sample or be differentiated through, but have no token sequence whose probability can be written down. HuggingFace TRL's GRPOTrainer assumes exactly that token sequence, which is why this layer is written against the adapter contract instead.

docs.title: Deliberately not here
docs.text:
• PPO/GRPO clipping, KL to a reference policy in logit space (the kl term is an L2 pull toward the initial weights in parameter space; 1e-3 in the class, 0.02 on the CLI).
  • Reward models trained from preferences, or reward from a downstream portfolio P&L.
  • Rollout servers (vLLM), sequence parallelism, distributed training.
  • Any claim that reward post-training improves forecast quality — that is 09_benchmark.md's job, and needs multiple seeds to say anything.

docs.title: Headline ranking
docs.text:
beat naive is the share of cells where the model's MASE beats the naive row scored on the same (series, span, horizon) cell - not MASE < 1: MASE's denominator is the in-sample mean |delta| of the train span, so on these series naive itself sits near 4.5 and a MASE < 1 test calls everything a loss. The ratio column is the median of per-cell mase_model / mase_naive, which is comparable across data paths (same bytes, same split, same denominator on both sides); raw median MASE is scoped to this pass. ctx prints the context lengths actually used - different ctx is a different measurement. win is the number of windows sampled per cell, and --max-windows draws them uniformly at random from the test span, so the window count is part of the measurement, not a knob: switching seed at 8 windows moves naive's own MASE ~55% median (max 100%) and the paired model/naive ratio ~12% (max 25%); at 32 windows those fall to ~21% and ~7% (measured 2026-11-27 on four arena series, same bytes, same code). Worse than noise: the share is a threshold on that noisy ratio, and the ratio sits just above 1, so a small window count inflates it.
